text: Once, Father Charalambos approached me after the service and asked, 'Do you know the Jesus Prayer?' I silently pointed to the prayer rope on my wrist. 'Well,' he said, 'and do you know how much one ought to pray?' 'Perhaps every day, every three hours…' I said uncertainly. 'All the time,' he replied in a didactic voice.

Once, when asked about how the Lord answers our prayers, Fr. Alexey replied: “In different ways.” It is a pithy and true response. Indeed, this work of mine is dedicated to that very notion. The world reveals itself to everyone in its own way. The subject of this book is simple: the phenomenology of experience. How we feel this world with our hearts and perceive it through our senses; how He speaks to us through what is heard. In psychiatry, there is even a term for this—‘ideas of reference’—which is how we see in films like *Bruce Almighty* that the world is addressing us: through text atop banners, billboards along the road, or, as in one Hollywood film, from the cells of Excel spreadsheets. Sometimes we hear our conscience distinctly—a ‘still small voice,’ as Spielberg often says in interviews (or the inner voice responsible for the spark of his films). In Gibson’s film about the battle on the ridge, the protagonist Desmond, a field medic, cries out to the Lord when all have abandoned the battlefield: ‘What do you want of me? I can't hear you!’—until suddenly, in the distance, he hears a voice call out, ‘Medic! Where’s the medic?’ Sometimes, the answer rings out from without.

Everyone speaks of this inner voice as well. Natalia Leonidovna Trauberg often used the expression ‘the angels whispered it.’ Vizbor has an entire song titled ‘Many-Voicedness’ dedicated to the voice within. The Romans believed in a voice that warned of and foresaw events—the voice of a ‘benevolent God,’ as my university lecturer once put it. The monk Dmitry Pershin, in one of his talks, identified the ability to hear this voice as one of the cornerstones of life.

The image of the wolf had haunted me since the very beginning of my journey. I had met family B., whose daughter gave me a set of gifts, among which was a small rubber bracelet. It bore the words ‘Winter is coming’ in white letters against a black background—quite ominous—and an engraving of the predatory head of an untamed wolf (lovers of *Game of Thrones* will recognize its origin, though I did not at the time). For me, it became a symbol of resolve, aiding in my maturation from a ‘little puppy,’ tamed by the communal life of Moscow.

Once, I was staying with my mother in Wales, and I decided it was time to leave. I rose and went to her room, intending to say goodbye before a short trip to a monastery or elsewhere, when my mother told me of an amazing dream she had. She said that in it, I was a domestic dog, tamed, but then suddenly I turned into a wolf and wandered off somewhere. I was so touched by this dream that I stayed for some time longer.

Later, when I finally left that town, a woman on the train, my seat neighbor, gave me a detective novel about medieval monks she had just finished. A year later, I chanced upon an Asian writer in Georgia; she had arrived from China and was busy approaching passersby at a bus stop in Tbilisi in search of a bookstore. I reached into my backpack, pulled out a slightly battered, crumpled book with a wolf on the cover, and gave it to her. We met two days later—she had already finished reading it—and she was so grateful that she later sent me letters from the road, during her journey around the world. In gratitude, Iris spent a wonderful day with me walking through local churches, and later, she even found herself by chance in the same temple with me, where she stood—despite not being Orthodox—directly before St. Nicholas. She also gave me a small scorpion keychain and a note that read, I believe, ‘Win like a wolf, without fighting.’

I have always been struck by the story of Iason Badridze, who lived among a wolf pack for more than two years. Once, while I was sitting in a hospital waiting room in Georgia, a talkative patient approached me; her mother was a publisher who had released his books. This, too, became a sign of sorts for me.

A sign is also a way of answering our prayers. A well-known Russian monk once said: ‘In order to make a choice, prayer is necessary. To make the right choice, and for God to provide the right person, strong prayer is needed.’ I believe this, combined with Papa Haralampios’s advice, is the key to perceiving the world as a symphony—harmonious and springing from the heart, where all is interconnected and logical. Once, I encountered a man who stood at a busy intersection, arms spread toward the converging roads, eyes shut, standing that way for several seconds. Perhaps he was praying, or trying to hear.

While living in Moscow, I happened to read many spiritual books, as I was doing little else. For the most part, these were books by Anthony of Sourozh. There were also Fr. Sergei Ovsiannikov’s *A Book About Freedom*, Maxim Trudolyubov’s book on the church institution, and others given to me by my confessor.
I read the article ‘Without Notes’ by Anthony of Sourozh, regarding his call to monasticism and his communion with his spiritual father.

We were riding with my sister in a black taxi; it was dawning on the streets. Zhenya was literally falling asleep on my shoulder, yet she continued to respond to my fiery speeches about how I longed for change, for ‘somewhere in the cosmos,’ for some special destiny, to find my footing after years of stillness… I spoke of my fears and, at the same time, my hopes, recalling the story of Metropolitan Anthony… The story of his spiritual father, his later return to his mother… And obedience in general… It all struck me, called to me, and frightened me. ‘But how—how I wish it could be for me as it was for him!’ I prayed.

It was then that Zhenya, half-asleep, suddenly uttered the phrase: ‘Perhaps it will be that way for you, too.’ We were driving to the airport.

I knew she was comforting me. A secret of some sort reflected like an echo in the car window.

Then began my mysterious and marvelous journey to Cyprus, where I spent several months without a map or a phone, trying to rely entirely on chance and the people around me. I was fortunate; I traveled the entire island and worked in a restaurant. This is how it was…

I went to Cyprus because I associated Greece with bodily vitality. Having received an invitation to a birthday in London, I found myself first there, then in Wales, in the house where I grew up. A good acquaintance of ours, who lived in the apartment below us, a family friend and, incidentally, the world’s first tightrope walker, suddenly called me over for a talk: ‘You know,’ he said, ‘who can help you right now? Not your first sister, Anya, but the second. Consult with her.’
And for some reason, I kept thinking of her all the time.

I felt that nothing was in vain. Something in Hussein’s words pointed to the non-randomness, the importance of this conversation. Perhaps it was happening only in my head, like this entire story (for we do indeed tell them to ourselves), but perhaps someone is telling them along with us? I do not know.

Once, in a shop in the city of Bath—a medieval town of astonishing beauty, with its wondrous basilicas, Roman baths, and Gothic cathedrals—I stepped into a bookstore and saw, sitting on a shelf, a tiny guidebook to modern Greece and a primer on the Greek language. In this discovery, nestled within that small, antiquarian shop, I wove the narrative of my own quest for adventure: a desire to break free from the familiar milieu of Moscow, that metropolis, and reach toward some semblance of a healthy life. I longed for this micro-prophecy—this small book found by chance—to be fulfilled, and for my desire to become renewed to truly take root in reality. Yet, I had almost no money in my pocket. I believe I had about twenty euros left, and that was all. Having nothing else, I relied on my intuition; I had previously sought work in Swansea, but I did not wish to linger long where I had once grown up—in the ghost-city of my childhood. I wanted to move on. I had never fit in; I never felt at home in that small, provincial seaside town.

The book on the Greek language seemed to beckon me, whispering, 'Go.' But Cyprus proved closer to my heart than Greece, for some of my friends were already there.

Following a conversation with my sister, and acting upon her advice, I found myself on a plane bound for Cyprus. The tickets were for Paphos. It was New Year’s, and I believe the pilot even offered his congratulations to the passengers, while I flew off alone toward lands unknown to me.

Why did I do it? What devilishly foolish thought propelled me into this leap into the void with twenty euros in my pocket and nothing more? Was it that I simply did not think of what lay ahead, or did a manic phase of consciousness make itself known? Or was it that I yearned so desperately to break out of my former, ossified existence—like a body frozen in Pompeii—and in doing so, to survive?

And here I stand by a station hotel, unadorned, simple, the cheapest I could manage to find, wandering along the embankment of the lovely city of Paphos. Without a cent in my pocket.

A neighbor of mine from Moscow lived in Paphos, and I sensed the possibility of a meeting. But for now, I decided to call a family friend and teacher to ask what I should do. Tanya was the only person on Skype—and in all of Moscow—to whom I could tell of my sudden idea; no one else could know. I felt something mysterious in the air, as if I had stepped into a cloud. While on the plane, I seemed to know intuitively that I would have to call her the moment I had the chance. For some reason, I felt as if this were our shared journey; I thought specifically of her (and indeed, to whom else should I recount such a thing if not to her—this followed naturally from our history).

Now, I needed a place to stay; I had no money to travel further, and no money for this hotel. Night was falling deep, and I knew neither the city nor the language of the place where I had found myself. Moreover, I was determined not to use the maps on my phone—such was my enthusiastically 'churched' period—due to an inability to use those technologies that had grown so tiresome and which seemed to impoverish life. I wanted to see and savor my impressions more clearly, to discern the misty world around me without avoiding it through an inward retreat into a screen. I had lived for too long as if 'locked away,' yet all around was still a dead end—streets that perpetually transformed, killing the sense of home. I had to keep this adventure a secret, to sever old ties. Only then could something radically new occur. A true journey.

— It’s me. — I frantically tried to reach her through the interference of the Wi-Fi signal, which the miraculous hotel receptionist provided for free at my special request. For a moment, I froze, struck by the thought that I had, for the first time in my life, reached such an exotic locale.

— No one knows, I haven't told a soul. I simply had to do this—I felt as if I couldn't do otherwise. — I insisted into the receiver. — I need your help. I’m in Cyprus!

The connection cut out again. I stood, penniless, at the only spot where a faint signal could be caught. Later, Tanya would tell me that there is a university in Cyprus, a decent one, and that an acquaintance of hers had even managed to train there as a psychologist. And this was my unfinished gestalt. That is how I conceived the plan to enroll in that university as well, which I did—though, alas, only for the sake of appearances; after a couple of months, I would have to leave the island due to changing plans.

— I urgently needed your help! To stay at a hotel for the night. Do you hear me? — The connection was barely there. I tried to compress my thought into the clearest, shortest possible message.

Finally, she answered, though the line was breaking up, asking in bewilderment what I was doing in Cyprus and how I had ended up there. The last time Tanya had heard from me was back in Moscow. She had heard nothing of my galloping through Europe with a suitcase, which had begun in Moscow over a month ago. Much water had flowed under the bridge since then. Through the rustle of the corrupted connection, I heard a clear, negative response:

— No. You won't get any money! — I was lost. Yet, at the same time, I was gladdened by her answer: she knew what was right—and that intonation calmed me.

— I will be very interested to talk to you, to find out what is happening—to hear your story. — I was very glad even for the refusal. It was a kind of anchor—I didn't care, even though I was thoroughly broken and in a difficult situation. I don't know, simply hearing her voice. An affirmative, firm, and self-sufficient message... Even if it was negative. I was not alone.

Near the wall of a cheap hotel, like a vagrant, with empty pockets. And her answer was such that there was no arguing with it at all... Later, we often spoke while I was there; it was such an experience of self-discovery. Tanya is a psychologist.

***

The woman at the reception turned out to be Russian-speaking; I was terribly lucky. We later became friends, and by a miracle, I managed to exchange the small bill left in my trousers right there. They showed me the way to my room (God knows how I had enough—perhaps it did cost those very 20 dollars I had), lent me a charger (I had to charge the damn phone after all), and I, finally calmed, set off for the 'burrow' they had given me. I had just enough money for that one night; the hotel was not at all expensive... I tried to call a friend to ask him to book something, but something went wrong with the reservation—in the sad outcome, he was unable to help me. I was obsessed with the idea of living through this leap on my own, without being a burden—how tired I was of that existence in Moscow, of unemployment and sloth. This was a qualitatively opposite step, a challenge to myself. I could not even conceive of asking, as I had before.

Now I had a friend—in the person of a family acquaintance who knew of my journey—and an ally in the receptionist, a comrade who could not help but was nonetheless perpetually responsive. I needed nothing else. I was still alone, as to all of them—it seemed to me—I could not leap across the abyss; I was gathering something slowly, grain by grain, like a story—a unique, world-distant narrative, like a hero's journey. It was reckless. Heroic and incredibly spontaneous, and at the same time, desperate. Something had literally pushed me out of my Moscow life. A kind of wild rejection of inertia, framed by fear. I cut away fear, as if out of hopelessness. The truth is, one could no longer go on like that. But I could not tell my family or relatives about the trip either—I didn't want to. This was my story, the path to maturity.

***

In the hotel lobby, I met a guy and a girl. They were from Switzerland, I believe—though I don't remember for certain—but they were definitely from Europe. The guy, as it turned out, was seriously interested in theology, and the girl was training as a modern dancer. I took a strong liking to both of them.

He was in his twenties, yet his gaze was surprisingly adult, perhaps even overly mature... He told me he was on a mission with the Lutheran church, of which he was a member, and that he undeniably loved everyone (which he felt necessary to announce to all present with pride; and not just to me, but also to the aforementioned girl who spoke Russian at the reception).

At first, it seemed a little naive to me—after all, in Moscow, we have been warned since childhood about such provocative behavior, haven't we?—but then I discerned in him a mature, grown man, perhaps someone on an important path of seeking. He talked to me and inquired with bright interest; he spoke of friends planning to go on a mission to Russia, of the differences in traditions—naturally, he was particularly interested in how our Orthodox Church differed from his own, the Protestant one. We spoke with him about the joy of children who have found parents, and whether people have a right to that before the face of the Lord, especially in such a difficult moment in history.

He insisted that, yes, they do; that one must sing songs, laugh, and smile—for we, he insisted and never tired of telling me, are children of God! Suddenly, he shared a deeply personal story about his deceased brother, whose death had taught him and his entire family a radically new attitude toward life and had prompted them to a profound faith. In that moment, he sounded very serious, and the feigned exaltation that I had previously perceived completely faded from his face and tone.

I grew to love his unusual, unfeigned courage, which allowed him not only to fight against circumstances (something I, having just left Moscow, was perfectly trained to do) but, while maintaining a spirit of resistance against all evil, to smile, laugh, and rejoice, proclaiming the love of God for them like some joyful mantra.

At the conclusion of our conversation—we were still standing in the lobby—he suddenly turned to me with his slightly naive smile and said (as if piercing me with a needle): 'Remember, it is normal to want to be something more than you are, but you are already “complete”; even now, as the Creator’s design.' (For some reason, these words did not sound like a customary 'mantra' for him...). 'Besides, you are obligated to rejoice! Believe me, it will help you.' And, finally, 'Do you know what is dearest to me in the teaching of Christ?'—I was exhausted by the conversation, stood like a post, and listened, and he suddenly seemed unusually large. 'That it teaches about our relationship with the Father, thus making us His children. We can address Him as His children.'

I heard his words as a sign. This settled in my feelings in a special way, for I was at the peak of my own quest for a path to God, trying with all my might to reach toward the Most High, to His likeness (this is within our capabilities—for it is commonly believed that in response to faith, the Lord grants us the gifts of the Kingdom of Heaven, sometimes even here) to become more mature and better. To reach for the 'golden city' in all its height.

Is it truly possible to rejoice already? Is it permitted? In Russia, I thought, we do not like to rejoice without reason, and with that thought, I went out for a walk.

I practically never used local maps while traveling—as I have already said—and I tried not to read any signs; I liked asking people about the simplest things: about transportation, about food—what was tastier... In time, even thinking that one could just open a map and not bother anyone with conversation became repugnant to me—I realized that in doing so, I was avoiding not only the conversation itself, but participation in life as a whole. And I liked people! There is so much happiness in them, so many variations of it. I simply could not trade this world for a phone.

And so, a wonderful, high-spirited Italian woman who was renting a room in the same hotel as me told me during breakfast where to go and which bus to take. At the Kiniras Hotel (of which I shall speak later), they served a wonderful breakfast every morning consisting of cereal and homemade jams made from exotic fruits and berries—the owner changes the selection once a week. I finished eating and soon followed the advice of the middle-aged Claudia: I walked to a bus stop with the beautiful name Caravella, where I boarded a bus heading to the Paphos embankment. But where did I get the money? I didn't have any, but I was helped by a friend living nearby in Cyprus, whom I managed to reach. I will explain everything.

The embankment of the city turned out to be a beautiful place. All around are restaurants with all sorts of mysterious seafood for every taste; right by the crashing waves stands a medieval castle, the property of the city. There, one can also see ancient frescoes of astonishing beauty... Which I did not get to see—alas, tickets cost money, and at that moment I had none at all... But I know of these frescoes from the words of wonderful Italians, fellow guests of Cyprus just like me, whom I met at that hotel. I was, undoubtedly, in a state of some euphoria from what I had seen and wanted to record every step.

I did not yet know how beautiful it would be, and when the bus arrived at its destination, I was stunned by the landscape that appeared before my eyes. 'This is what it’s all for (meaning: my Path),' I thought! 'For all this beauty.' Just like BG said—a terrifying power.

My next destination, and for a substantial amount of time, turned out to be the Kiniras Hotel—a wonderful, uniquely individual place. I did not choose it; for me, it was chosen by that very friend who had already been living on the island for some time, managing a small business in Russia... I was no longer to wander from one place to another... Andrei booked me a room in a random hotel—this was not so much a hotel as a family-run, homemade-spirited bed & breakfast—and it turned out to be the best establishment of its kind in Paphos. It was run by George Gregoriou, a capricious and literally crazy man, ready to do everything with his own hands. The Italian woman who pointed me toward Caravella was from there. We ate breakfast together in the mornings... In the Kiniras Hotel, everything was different from everywhere else. Art objects, guests, 'Lamb!', 'Chicken!' and the owner... and even the weather behind the clouds was different. As if it were a fairy-tale place. In Kiniras, there were decorative objects on the stone floor and along the walls, positioned very unexpectedly (the owner was, among other things, an artist!), and many, many paintings hanging in every corner. The hotel rooms also contained one, sometimes more, paintings of a perfectly decent appearance—all, as it turned out, the work of the owner.

'Chicken!', 'Pork!' announced Gregoriou, making the rounds of his domains with the gloomy yet confident air of a man who has mastered his craft, like Gordon Ramsay in a television broadcast, advancing into the depth of the hall—to where the kitchen is located and, it seems, one woman works. The dishes served at Kiniras are all exquisite, the meat is pointedly tender, the side dishes healthy and tasty—predominantly vegetables. And this place is a family one.

I noticed during my trip that the better the place where you stay, the more pleasant the guests and the food, the less, as a rule, is known about it! This rather strange tendency is, perhaps, quite adequate to the unreasonable world in which we live today—where everything is bought and sold remotely, without human contact, without relationships; where our main concern is to help those who are far away. Of course, they need help, and there are grounds for this; it would be foolish to argue against it, but first and foremost, we bear responsibility for those who are near, do we not?—for their joy and mood, for their happiness. Perhaps this is harder than helping children distant from us, or getting rid of plastic bags, and, perhaps, it is more important for us specifically. I feel sorry for those who are far away, too... But life provides so many chances to help those who are near that there may not be enough strength for the others.

***

The center of Limassol was like an enchanted city, saturated with narrow forks and shops selling handmade goods. Soap and coffee—both locally ground (Cypriot coffee) and from the fruit of a tree resembling a dried banana! (the carob tree—from which they make practically everything here: from coffee to a spread for bread, which is wondrously tasty). And in taste, it does not differ much from ordinary Cypriot coffee; ground carob coffee is somewhat similar to beige-colored cane sugar. In general, a wonderful merchant spoke to me about all this; he produces these numerous goods himself, partly bringing them from his home in Greece.

There, he mainly produces excellent wine—he is a professor at a Greek university, by the way. A real, bona fide professor of winemaking. Now his son manages the business in Cyprus, and he himself visits his son from Greece, where he produces his goods. The carob tree grounds made a unique impression on me, a wondrous astringent drink reminiscent of coffee, yet self-sufficient and completely unique... It is closest to chicory, but even that cannot be compared at all... Astringent and very mild. This coffee has its own identity: a mild yet strict, astringent, and tender fruity taste. Here is their business card:

In Limassol, I lived in a wonderful hostel. But I learned of it in a church—one of the most hidden and touching places I knew in that city. It became very significant to me. The Church of St. Anthony, and nearby, closer to the seashore, a small chapel where icons of St. George the Victorious are hung on four walls. The rector, clad in a modest dark blue cassock (I do not know his rank), accompanied me there, treated me with exceptional attention, guided me, and showed me everything. And he stood quietly nearby, as they do at confession, as genuine people 'are present' beside us in important moments.

While I was walking along the embankment—right after I left the first church, St. Anthony’s—he met me. How it coincided that he seemed to be waiting for me there at the threshold of the chapel, or ended up in both places, or our 'traffic' simply coincided—I do not know. He stood and smiled, with an open smile and warmth. But he was as if entirely transparent and absorbed in his inner affairs.

St. George’s chapel, as it turned out, was also his; it was like a tiny cell, two or four square meters, I don't remember, very modest, with one censer and an astonishing, angelically warm atmosphere of a monastic cell. It stood near antique ruins where numerous cats wandered back and forth, and not far away, seals lay about. As I already said, it was hung with icons of St. George the Victorious, of the most varied sort and origin, such that no empty space remained on the wall, yet it did not look cumbersome or pompous—entirely modest. Dark, medieval-looking, faded, worn, bright and shining. In it was an extraordinary, to my mind, spirit. In general, when this priest showed me the chapel first and then the church, I took a particular liking to them.

***

An hour earlier, when I was particularly vexed, distressed by my departure from Moscow, dreaming for some reason of returning to Moscow, I suddenly turned from the altar and saw that a local church servant (a grumpy Greek old man) greeted a young girl (Lisa from Russia) who had looked in for some reason.

I was incredibly surprised that precisely in this soul-wounding moment, when I was in such need of help, and I stood at the altar of a beautiful, hitherto unfamiliar church, she suddenly walked in—quiet, arriving on a bicycle. We stood at the entrance to the church. She told me how she had come from Moscow, that she worked in Moscow somewhere as an English teacher, and her brother was a theater student. She was like a relative! How wonderful that was! To receive news from home once more, in such a remote, unexpected, and personal, intimate place. I thought that my prayers had suddenly been heard and she appeared before me with her bicycle, I don't even remember exactly what she was wearing, perhaps a summer dress. After all, I had stood at the altar and zealously prayed for help, for money, and for guidance. Movement.

In general, we exchanged warm phrases; Lisa recommended a hostel to me, which she had once been advised to visit—'Trip Yard Hostel'—and testified that it was an excellent place to stay, to take a breather within the city limits. I was very glad for this lead on the Trip Yard... And she said that one could stay there for a short while for free, in case of special need. But first, I went to the embankment, inquiring in all places along the way about vacancies and work, and, relying on intuition, entering various cafes with a printed sheet of my resume.

A similar story once happened to me during my university studies, where I also had to look for earnings, and then I spent a hundred such flyers before I received a job offer at a cafe. That time, it seems, at one of the restaurants, I was asked to pour wine in an aristocratic manner, as true masters do, holding the bottle by the bottom, in a fancy restaurant, and I did not succeed...

***

At the hostel, I met all its wonderful inhabitants, multi-instrumentalists (they live in it as if in a commune, and some others, volunteers, remaining practically as masters of the establishment, can live in it, rotating among themselves; volunteering in this way). Unfortunately, it was impossible to find work. I went through practically all the establishments that were there, but I could not find a job—the only place that would take me immediately was this restaurant that was still under construction, not far from the Nero cafe on *** Street! I got the position at the brothel through sheer persistence, shouting and arguing with its senior manager. In general, I had to work as long as I could, until the owner kicked me out for disobedience—and to leave the hostel soon after due to the inability to pay...

I had to deceive the hostel owners only once, as I had nowhere to go—the money had run out and I desperately needed a cot... It was pouring rain. I had already spent nights on end waiting for the restaurant owner to pay me the promised money after all... I slipped into the hostel, as it was always open, and lay down in my former spot... I leave the name of the hostel here, hoping that people will see it and, in this way, I will pay for the one night I did not pay for. Trip Yard Hostel, Limassol.

***

However, after being fired from the restaurant, housing in Limassol was found with surprising speed... The son of George Gregoriou, the owner of the hotel in Paphos, introduced me to his friend, with whom I lived for some time.

In addition, I managed to help a friend of mine in Larnaca who had previously paid for my accommodation in Kinyras. We recorded a masterclass with an Israeli specialist in Tai Chi and other martial arts, utilizing my skills as a video editor…

We were on a special trip, and I felt relieved and more comfortable afterward. I had saved money for housing, but I had to give half of it away in an unusual manner—literally leaving my beloved computer behind in lieu of payment to the landlord. He had a small business and needed a computer at that moment, much like I did. It had been a gift from my father.

My friend called me, and I learned that a mutual acquaintance of ours was expected to be in roughly the same area the next day, accompanying her father on his theatrical tours; I was overjoyed at this and set off to see her.

Leaving my friend, who had been brought to the island by the whims of fate, I saw no clear prospects ahead. It seemed to me that everything most valuable and dear had been left behind, and before me lay an abyss of uncertainty.

I could not imagine how to bridge this chasm. There was no place for me behind me anymore—I wanted to return, but where to, and to do what? Which meant that ahead there had to be something of which I was yet unaware. The taxi driver drove calmly, at no more than 60 km/h, on the road back to Limassol… I did not look very joyful.

Suddenly the taxi driver began to speak to me—he was from Georgia. He said that one must have a goal in life, and that to reach it, one need only concentrate and not retreat, and then (he suddenly shifted to a religious theme) the Lord will surely grant everything you could ever desire. He then told me several stories—about how, on a mountain, his ancestors once saw a man in whom they recognized a famous saint who had lived long, long ago… Then he suggested that I pray at home, making the sign of the cross over the water in which I bathed, and always to use the word “Christos”; he shared some stories from his own personal pilgrimage experience, if one could call tourist drives through the monasteries of Cyprus in a private car by such a name. He was very sincere in his conviction, as well as in his straightforwardness and, apparently, in the authenticity of his tales; and in his concept of achieving success with the help of God. We parted ways as soon as the taxi reached its destination. “Here is my number,” he said, giving me a business card in case I too wanted to take a tour of the island’s monasteries. Of course, not for free, but I think for a modest sum. I needed to sleep. I returned to the walkthrough room at my friend’s place, where my computer had been, and lay down, recalling the sudden encounter with my friend from Moscow. “The morning is wiser than the evening,” I remembered as usual, and soon fell asleep. There was still plenty of wind in my head…

I longed for something more; I liked Limassol, and I had already managed to settle in a bit. Everyone knew me, and I had managed, somehow or other, to get established, to work a little, and even to put down roots in this house, where one could stay with the Thai girls—the landlord’s neighbors—and a parrot (or maybe there were two birds, I don’t recall) for some time in perfect peace. The sun spilled marvelously onto the terrace there… And the birds sang. Quiet, philosophical conversations. Truth be told, I slept there by crawling into the narrow space between a table and a mattress lying in the hallway area… It was the only free spot.

Thoughts visited me of somehow staying and leaving only much later, having first invited all my truly wonderful friends from Moscow to visit. Living in a more or less calm state (since there was housing, glory to God), I even found some places, like Russian schools, with which I wanted to collaborate and where I could teach… I chose, for instance, a school where I would go to learn how to drive.

But for some reason, the thought crossed my mind to study, to finish the Gestalt psychological training that had been left incomplete some time ago. Tanya—my teacher and sensei—recommended a university, and I decided that since my services were no longer needed at Bordello (for now, I had only found a children's center where I could teach theater arts in Russian), then I might as well leave. Truth be told, I again overestimated my capabilities (20 euros in savings was clearly insufficient for such a step).

I planned to arrive in Nicosia, settle into a hostel somewhere, and conquer the city—or at least, get enrolled.

After thinking a bit, I decided my affairs with Stelios were complete and jumped on a bus from Limassol (I forgot the name of the stop; it was a landmark and hard to find, somewhere near the police station—I remember that) to the city of Nicosia. In short, I flew off on that bus, continuing my journey.
I left Limassol for good, again practically without money, having neither housing nor funds for existence in Nicosia, feeling that if I could hold on, something within me would continue to change or emerge. I planned to earn money, as the prospects were greater in Nicosia. Although, everything turned out to be far more complicated…


***

Whenever I felt a particular surge of weariness, God would send me some new distraction. For instance, when I was riding the bus to Nicosia, my seatmate turned out to be a former goalkeeper who had played for Turkey. He showed me pictures from his past life (he no longer plays, having retired) and all his children. For some reason, he wanted to make my journey as comfortable as possible: adjusting the back of my seat, for example, because I was a bit tired. (I myself despised thinking about such things; I tried to bear everything stoically, paying no attention to my physical condition). My neighbor, however, tried to anticipate my desires, offered food, and asked if I was comfortable. At one point, he suddenly began talking about a hotel we were passing, where the first casino in the Cypriot territory of the island was about to open. He poked his finger in various directions and laughed, pointing out the beauties and talking about what a fun and carefree occupation card playing was! “Look,” he said, pulling a bill from his wallet, “I put in 20 Turkish lira”—he waved the paper bill (on the Turkish side, playing in casinos was permitted), “and then—bam!—he said, and today I have 200 in my wallet” (he showed me—it was indeed two hundred). And he laughed. “I mean, you don’t need much! So it’s not a sin. And what if you get lucky? Why not! If not, well, nothing terrible.” He looked like Adriano Celentano. So light, friendly, and carefree. “Fix this, put that there—it’ll be more comfortable.” He expressed his care. He gave many necessary pieces of advice; in essence, he guarded me against myself.

***

My favorite priest from the Faneromeni church, when I asked him what I should do, would repeat, “Do as you feel.” — “I don’t know, just do as you feel.” These encouraging words were like honey on wounds for me. I immediately understood what to do because I trusted myself—knowing that wherever my conscience led me, as long as I was doing nothing forbidden or with malicious intent, I could trust it; for, in essence, it is not just intuition that acts, but God Himself acting in this way, together with it. With this realization, warmed by his radiant, stout warmth and the priest’s wise parting words, I moved further and further along on my journey. The city was full of amazing twists and turns, on every one of which stood churches from deep antiquity with relics inside.

In the Faneromeni (Mother of God) Church in the very center, where that same priest was, I also witnessed an amazing celebration.
On one of the first days I stepped into the Faneromeni church, a wondrous event was taking place. A queue of parishioners stood near the images of two saints: Pamphilius and Flavian (the Patriarch of Constantinople); the clergy conducted a special service, as it seemed to me, after which the people in line, as they approached the icons, received a little rose water (actual water from roses) in their palms from a ladle. Everything around was fragrant. It seemed that roses had been scattered, spilled everywhere (though there was nothing but a drop of rose water from the pitcher); only later did I learn that this is how the Greek Church honors the memory of these two remarkable men.

***

“You don’t have to like it,” another priest I knew told me. It doesn’t matter if you are happy or not—that was his thought. And I accepted it; for a person must forget about himself, and then we have a chance to see something worthwhile—beyond our limits, including even our own destiny. Only by ceasing to think about ourselves, by losing ourselves (which does not mean losing a careful attitude toward oneself as a vessel of the Lord and not washing in the mornings!), can we truly discern what we are being called to (Greek: κένωσις, kenosis—meaning emptying in the name of Christ); and not just what we want at this day and moment. We begin to see where we are needed most now, and the question of destiny stops being so tricky—you simply do what must be done. The next hour—not just the day, but the hour!—truly, it takes care of itself.

Further on, the next task will open up, the next conversation in which something will become clear. And beware if you suddenly want something “of your own”—it is most likely a road to nowhere. Unless, of course—which sometimes happens—you have been given an opportunity to rest—a real respite—and you know for certain that this time is yours. Then use it to the maximum and with joy.

Next was another chapter—I went into a small shop on Ledra Street; in English, they are called grocery stores, but in terms of assortment, it is more of a kiosk (albeit not in the open air!), or a *periptero*. And later I wandered without money for ten days, and spent five on the street, and it was important for me to record this here… Each night I ended up under the awning of a restaurant. There was no money, and I was losing everything. At the “Periptero” they gave me the coordinates of some Jewish community that helps, but no one was there. But most importantly, there was still Father Haralampios, who gave me both money for the road and a task-blessing, regarding where and how to move… I spent my last money in the lowest-level hotels while I had it, while simultaneously looking for work. I had to live on the street for five nights or so, and believe me, my friends, for the transgressions I had committed before, a greater punishment is unimaginable, especially when a torrential rain is pouring and the temperature drops to minus three. I survived even that, sitting under the awning of a McDonald’s, from which I was eventually chased away. And that’s not to mention that when I was still in Limassol for the first few days, some new acquaintances made in a cafe led me to an abandoned hotel where the walls were destroyed, and the hotel itself was occupied by Pakistani homeless people. For twenty bucks, I had to spend the night in the same room with them—they slept in a recess in a destroyed wall.


The idea was that while I was wandering, it was as if God were watching, and I was doing all this partly to test Him. I wanted to be sure that He was truly standing guard over my well-being. Of course, I believed, and I believed in the invisible, the inscrutable. Unfortunately, God will not help if you throw yourself into the fire without thought, or He will teach you a lesson. My arrival there was such a lesson… I sought meaning, but I threw myself too abruptly into the abyss without relying on my own strength either. Without the help of reason, fueled only by flame, and signals were visible everywhere, as in the film *Bruce Almighty*—on the road—go there, do not be timid, do not go, take care of yourself… I felt, nevertheless, as if in a cradle. In God’s hands. Hope did not abandon me, and every day was something sharply different from the previous ones. An adventure. It was impossible to stay in one place; that was what the monk from Russia, Ioan Guaita, had taught me.

***

In the Archbishopric—the central building in Nicosia, almost like the Vatican in Rome—I found myself on the recommendation of a woman of Georgian descent who worked for many hours in that very *periptero* shop. This wonderful woman, who helped me at various stages of my journey, suddenly mentioned this place—saying, go (or rather, walk, as it’s quite close!) to the place that is here; tell them your story and let them help you—with money, advice, anything at all. So I decided, since it was suggested, not to delay and to head there—through winding alleyways; it was only a fifteen-minute walk in the indicated direction. Of course, I got lost, went the wrong way a few times, but in the end, I found the road and, at the conclusion of a long journey, ended up on the spot.

“Who are you?” asked a guy from the security booth sharply, right at the entrance to the building, almost lunging at me.

“I… uh… I’m here for this woman,”—the name was written on a crumpled piece of paper,—“she helps people like me who have ended up without money,”—I said, using an almost rehearsed phrase. “Can I get in touch with her somehow?!”
He seemed to wake up; he quickly jumped up, ran out of the booth, smiled broadly with his beard, and said: “What, ended up without a roof and without cash? Came to study?” he guessed. “I knew it—come here,”—and he grabbed the receiver of the rotary phone to call this woman who handles such cases. To call her from the posh, indescribably beautiful building from the mid-20th century, the Archbishopric.

Of course, at first, the woman refused me any help—and one can understand her!—but this guy, on the other hand, helped me a great deal. Having considerable connections within the Archbishopric (as he himself had once worked in that charitable position), he managed to secure me a practically instantaneous check that saved me at that moment. The check was signed directly by the archbishop. I even, barely having recovered from such luck, promised that I would name my child after this kind guy.

That same Chris (Haris) subsequently took me to a local barber, and then drove me to an acquaintance at a local pub—all right there, nearby. It turned out they needed waiters, and Mike—the local manager—offered me the job. But more on that later.

***

It must be said that despite being forced to live on the street, it was one of the most productive periods of my life, the events of which, like dominoes, multiplied and rushed one after another. I met the most amazing, interesting people, from university scholars to immigrant saleswomen… Many women from the Faneromeni church, meeting me somewhere on the streets, would give me money, donate to my living expenses, so to speak—sometimes even twenty euros; others helped me with a word or accompanied me to a neighboring church, say, to introduce me to the relics of the saints. It was like a seminary. In parallel, there were conversations about business and the most varied things with people met on this street. I remember how I was walking through the alleys, of which there are many in Nicosia, and three women, parishioners from Faneromeni, where I also went, were walking toward me. One of them immediately led me—or directed me, I don't remember now—to the church of St. Cassian… Another handed me an icon and advised me to pray to him for headaches. They also showed me a reliquary of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste and told me about them for a long time.

***

I was walking up a street in Nicosia and became thirsty. I went into the first establishment I came across, and it turned out to be a wonderful family business opened by two brothers. Because of this, its name contained two names, Michael and Angelo—and thanks to a play on words, the logo took on the outline of an angel. I went in and met one of the brothers, who was serving customers behind the bar himself. We started talking, and in the course of the conversation, it turned out that he was deeply interested in the development of his recently opened business and the topic of coffee production itself—it was not a simple matter for him; he was not indifferent to anything he did there. He travels the world to all sorts of seminars, trying to learn everything there is to know about coffee—what kind of beans are needed, how best to brew it, what vessels to use, and which coffee machines are best to acquire so that the taste of the coffee does not suffer. It was evident that he felt a genuine interest in what he was doing, and it gradually emerged that in the near future he planned to open another establishment—on the city’s central street. Of course, it is not simple, and one needs to recoup the costs of renting the space, which is not cheap, but as he told me, when he felt ready for such an expansion, he was suddenly offered a space with incredibly favorable terms, completely by chance. We talked a little about the role of chance in life; I drank my freshly brewed coffee, which was to my liking, and set off further to where I was headed. Nevertheless, their business card remained in my pocket, and I treasure it as a reminder that one can treat business with a warm, caring heart, rather than relying solely on potential profit. I was glad for this acquaintance.

***

Another of my conversations about business was with that very woman who worked in a small *periptero* grocery store on Ledra Street. Such *peripteros* are scattered all over Cyprus, but this particular one happened to be in my path when I was searching for work and housing. It was difficult for me to do so, knowing no one, and Nina provided me with selfless and invaluable help.

In the course of our acquaintance, I learned that she used to work in a laundry for a wonderful person (Nina was originally from Georgia, so most of our conversations in one way or another touched upon the history of her family left behind there, back home). She longed for home, but for ten years she had been working in a foreign land, earning money for her family, and had even married a local policeman—and the nearest police station where he once worked was right across the street from the shop.

We became very close friends; but the thought of the laundry she told me about wouldn’t leave me alone… It was a family laundry run by that very wonderful employer she spoke of—he treated all his employees like family; in fact, most of them were his family, so that was not surprising. Nevertheless, he accepted Nina into that circle, and by the time he tragically passed away, she was as dear a person to him as everyone else—his own relatives. It seemed to me that there was a certain incompleteness in this story, and so it turned out: Nina herself wanted, out of a sense of duty and responsibility for the life of this man—who was wonderful by her description—to open a laundry or to participate in the life of the very laundry where she had worked before his sudden passing. Now it was being run, I believe, by his daughter, but according to Nina, things were not going as well as before, and the place needed to be saved… But she could not bring herself to take that step—too many risks. Yes, it would have been a much better job than the one she had now, but she was afraid to intrude into other people’s family affairs, especially since if she failed to save the business, she would probably lose her current income and let her family down. But a strange feeling would not let me go, as if she were hesitating in vain: it seemed to me that everything would have worked out for sure if she had only tried—after all, all the odds were in her favor! She knew the owners perfectly well and the nature of the business itself, knew what steps to take, and even had some distant understanding (at the very least, the necessary mutual understanding) with his descendants, for whom the entire operation of this laundry was somewhat of a burden—after all, everyone has their own life, their own desires and affairs… But surely, on the contrary, her heart clearly ached for this establishment, for its future fate, and that means, as it seemed to me, she should have participated in it. But, unfortunately, due to practical circumstances and a lack of confidence in the financial stability of her own family, she rejected this idea and decided not to get involved—at least until better times… But when will they be, these better times? Can there ever be a convenient time for risk? But there is our sense of shared experience, and it, as it seemed to me then and seems to me still, is key—the main compass in the question of what we should do, and when. I hope that something will work out for her nonetheless.

The owner of the “Toni” hotel in the center of Nicosia also spent hours telling me about her father, who had previously owned this establishment; now, she herself sits for 12 hours behind glass in a compact glass booth standing behind the door on the street. It must be said that staying there is exceptionally pleasant—it is comfortable everywhere; she did the renovations herself, with sincere pleasure—selecting pictures, the laminate for each room, using the motif of London booths and buses, which resulted in some rooms being painted red. Others, blue. And others still, simply white. All of them are quite simple, but at the same time convenient, done with care, with the future of the family business in mind, by this one woman who dreams of turning an abandoned, barely maintained place with a large number of worn, untidy rooms into the best budget hotel in the center—the old city—of Nicosia! And, it seems to me, she has succeeded in much. At the very least, her kind charm and charisma have left their mark on her work—the place breathes with freshness and beckons one to come in. Although, of course, the facade of the premises where this booth is located could be changed, for it hardly reflects the current state of the interior… But that is only a matter of time! Such is the fate of a family business—it will necessarily change, and then change again.

For some time, I lived in the “Toni” hotel. From time to time, I would step out onto the balcony; from various sides, the hum from the mosques would drift, awakening the city from its slumber before anyone else. This sound would spread over the entire city, even over the sky, and it was impossible not to wake up to it; then I would take my things and, without looking back, head out of the hotel onto the street, where I anticipated the arrival of new adventures. At times, it seemed to me that it was not I, but some force pushing me out of the four walls into the light, with the hidden purpose of colliding with one person or another, one problem or another—I could not and did not want to resist this force and gladly submitted to it: what would happen next. The world was full of surprises that did not make one wait long!.. The most difficult thing was to find permanent, cheap housing—in which I could stay for a long time… I searched for such a refuge throughout the entire journey. By the way, I even managed to enroll in a university during these days, but that is a story for another time.

I longed to find meaning, and as soon as I set foot on Cypriot soil, I felt I had found it—not as something finished or final, but as a process, a pilgrimage drawing me toward it. Now every step, every word, every movement I made seemed full of purpose, significant for someone—for myself, yet as if for more than that alone—and everything that happened to me seemed far from mere chance. I could not fully explain why I did what I did, yet I had not the slightest doubt that it was right, no matter what occurred or what trials arose. I was ready for them, and I was glad.

Fri, 23 Mar. '18. Still on the island of Cyprus

The monastery, named for an ancient icon of the Mother of God (unlike most icons, the Holy Virgin is depicted here without Christ), is situated atop a high mountain. We reached it after an hour's drive with a remarkable monk who usually serves in a small, hidden church in the center of Nicosia. He agreed to take me there, as he is one of the monastery's own, though he serves remotely at the church assigned to them by the Machairas Monastery.

I was very fond of my traveling companion. Taciturn, barely speaking English, yet seeming to understand me and my mood perfectly even without words, this free spirit drove me along winding mountain roads. We swayed along those narrow paths, side to side, and when we arrived, I felt a cleansing sensation unlike any I had known before—perhaps that was the purpose of the winding path: to experience it, to leave behind all the worldly things that cling to the soul and memory, hanging on one's back like a pack, like iron chains. Now, I was at peace.

We paused halfway. The Machairas Monastery lies at an altitude of 1,000 meters, and getting there means traversing breathtaking vistas. As we drove, I watched—eyes wide open to the wind—all the landscapes, trees, and clouds rushing past as we rose above a deepening abyss, barely visible from the window at such speed. With every turn, I felt a new sense of relief, as if something passing us by outside was also, inevitably, taking place within us. I felt reborn, already unburdened. Although my luggage remained in the trunk of the car (that infernal suitcase with the rattling wheels). In short, by the moment we arrived, leaving behind the sacred place for the monks—where, in uncreated light, this icon, painted according to tradition by the Apostle Luke, was once discovered in a burning bush.
It was in the glowing bush that this miracle-working icon was found by the monks.

***

The gates opened, and we entered a walled complex resembling an ancient fortress, with detached dwellings, narrow lanes, and church annexes: there was a spacious refectory, a temple of wondrous appearance, a small guesthouse (with neat, lovingly maintained rooms for pilgrims), and a multitude of rooms for conversation and the various needs of the monastery. Not to mention the cells for the monks, though these were somewhat hidden from first sight—I never did fully grasp where they were.

We would meet the monks either at service or just before, at the entrance to the church where they would obediently gather; or at meals, where, despite the regular fast, they served delicious fish with couscous and a variety of nourishing food that always left one feeling light, all carefully prepared by the monks' own hands hours before the Liturgy. Everything consumed by the members of the monastic community, they grew and prepared themselves—they cleaned the fish, baked the pies, boiled and made the pasta, and at the end of it all, washed the mountains of dishes corresponding to the number of monks—there were certainly no fewer than thirty of them. It all looked like the boundless expanses of a magical Hogwarts.

They would sit down cautiously, trying to maintain an inner silence, but sometimes they would whisper to one another, smiling sincerely and nodding in unison—even to me. They sat at these long, wide tables, and at the command of the Abbot (who was reading the canon), they would suddenly begin their meal. It was a rite of wondrous beauty, in which I was happy to participate (several times a day, usually after the morning service); especially because, as I said, the food was excellent.

And it was a pleasure to see all those spiritually alive faces—despite the monotony and the black color of their vestments—faces of joyful people who had found their true place and calling. Each one present had their own biography, a unique path that had led them here, and this was clearly imprinted on every deep face that flitted lightly by.

Of those I came to know, besides the Abbot-in-residence, with whom we had a brief but unforgettable conversation, I spent most of my time with the remarkable Father Ignatius—who, it seems, had once lived in Moscow—which, incidentally, was also imprinted on his face—and an intelligent father of Greek descent who had once studied at a university in Great Britain. I was immediately pointed toward him as a particularly experienced and profound mentor (his modest, harmonious, and temperate spirit made a special impression on me), better educated than many others, and for that reason, I liked him at once. It is amazing that God always sends us exactly what we need, upon request. Unfortunately, we did not get to speak for long due to Father Nektarios' lack of time. Every time the opportunity arose, something would distract us—either him or me—and in response to my restless impulses and the question, "How, then, can we finally arrange our meeting?", he would quietly, peacefully reply, "Next time," and humbly walk away.

Father Ignatius, on the other hand, a short, acerbic Armenian, became a close friend at once, and we spent long periods in conversation, many hours it seems: he told me of his life, of the phenomenon of the Elders, of a multitude of miracles he had witnessed himself. Some struck me particularly—for example, he told me of a saint whose name I do not recall now, who once, under the influence of dark forces and in a state of mental obfuscation, attacked a young girl, molested her, and to avoid further shame, it seems, even killed her. This was the Venerable James the Faster. This story shocked me more than any other! Can one who has committed such a thing really be canonized? As it turned out, yes, it is possible—so profound was his subsequent repentance before the Lord, so greatly did he wish to be cleansed of the painful malady that had overcome him (so powerful, evidently, was the degree of his temptation) that, having finally defeated it through tearful repentance, he was later raised to the rank of saint. I found it hard to believe, to be honest, but Father Ignatius was so sincere, so thoroughly imbued with his own deep concern and genuine interest in everything, that the story sounded somehow different coming from his lips; just as direct and authentic, with the same power of repentance and standing before God that, perhaps, that saint from his tale had experienced. All his stories were imbued with this quality—a genuine humility and personal depth. It was an honor for me to speak with him, even though he would repeat incessantly that he was likely tiring me (he longed to speak with a Russian) and would try to end his tale each time—oh, he would lament, how talkative I am, when I should be silent!.. “I truly want, and strive to be silent, Yasha,” he would confess. And I deeply empathized with him. I grew very fond of Fr. Ignatius, and by the end, when I had to leave after three days (instead of two—I managed to stay at the monastery longer), I was moved almost to tears by our parting; all the more so because it was unknown at that moment when we might meet again. He was the only person in the monastery speaking to me in Russian and, despite all the controversial points in his stories, the closest—he became my guide into the life of this wondrous abode, for which I am deeply in his debt.

It is worth noting that the Abbot himself, a Greek stretched tall toward the heavens, could sometimes speak Russian (usually suddenly and unexpectedly). Broad-shouldered, of gigantic height, with a naive bald spot and a smile that never left his focused face, yet with the seriousness and even cunning inherent to an Abbot, he would walk past me and mockingly repeat like a mantra, “Patience, Iakovos” (that was what they called me in Greek)—and then, in passing as he walked away, in Russian: “Patience, prayer, glory to God.” I took these words as a rhythmic accompaniment and a mantra for everything that was happening, if not for my whole life—I so wanted to know something, to secure a meeting with him, to quickly resolve my pressing questions at the time—about housing and work—just to stay on Cyprus—and so, with great zeal and energy, I made myself known every time I saw him. The idea was that they might house me there or let me serve at the *metochion*, at that very church in Nicosia where the monk who drove me was from. He watched me, and everyone else, intently. And when, after our conversation, he repeated those words to me—all the more so in native Russian and, surprisingly, without the slightest accent (though, as far as I know, he barely knew Russian!)—with his unwavering, kind smile, I felt light again; I understood that, in essence, I had nowhere to hurry, that indeed, one must accept everything as it is and simply pray quietly. And so I did. At the end of my three-day stay, the monks generously gave me food for the road: vegetables, fruit, and thin corn tortillas to wrap it all in—what care they took!—and I set off further on my way. I left with nothing, from the point of view of the mission I had set for myself, but I was wonderfully equipped.
“Hey you, Hegel,” Mr. Mike asked me in his latest message, “are we going to work today or what? You’re on the shift from six o’clock and you’re still not here!”

I was back in the city, and work awaited. I rushed there as quickly as I could. And by the way, Mr. Mike, I haven’t read Hegel, and I’m not really inclined to right now. Perhaps he read him and found a resemblance in me? He was the owner of the cafe where I had found work—he could barely walk, limping on crutches, but he still rode a motorcycle.

I had to put on the uniform, tie the blue apron around my waist! To greet the walk-ins seeking either a conversationalist or a mug of yellow wheat beer. I don't like it. How do they drink it, especially in such quantities? It’s frightening to think! My colleague said, “strange, we have some kind of monk-in-the-making working here,” and laughed, and my boss, Mr. Mike, reacted with similar humor. It was interesting to work there; everywhere there were people, everywhere their voices and eyes—seeking one another in the bustle and noise, and lonely. By the way, about voices: Father Ignatius from Machairas once told me, during our long talk, that everyone’s voice is different from another’s—and it is truly so! If you hear the voice of someone you know or someone close to you, you recognize it immediately! Especially if it is someone you have not seen for a long time; and you say we are all of one mold—like digital copies—well, no. I don’t think I agree with that even one iota now, though the thought is tempting.

In Mr. Mike’s cafe, now run by his son, a young guy named Yanis worked. Well, one day, on a routine workday, I was sitting at a cafe table, outside, waiting for my shift. Usually, during this wait, we could ask for a free coffee or, say, an orange juice… as Mr. Mike used to say in American (he loved all those Bruce Lees and Williamses), “it’s on the house”—I asked for a frappe. On Cyprus, everyone drinks frappe exclusively. I don’t know why—first of all, it’s quite unhealthy, and second, there is much more elegant, deep, and textured, robust Cypriot coffee; but no, all the service staff drink this cold frappe for some reason, regardless of the weather. In short, I asked for just that, partly because it was easier to make (it uses a basic powder base), and partly because I needed to refresh myself. I had been on my feet for many hours and was quite tired. And the volume of the drink was several times that of a cappuccino. In short, I sat at the corner table where we usually sat and drank my frappe, occasionally smoking and rolling my own cigarettes. Then Yanis came over and asked why I had such a sour face… Was it really so sour? Is it so noticeable? And indeed, I felt as if a heavy stone were hanging around my neck, pressing down on me and seemingly choking me… And I didn't know how to handle it. After all, I was here all alone, like in a war; I had no one to turn to when something was wrong.

But suddenly Yanis—this twenty-year-old womanizer who would tell me about his romantic adventures time and again—suddenly showed me incredible sensitivity.
“Why so down?” he asked.
“I don’t know,” I said—though in fact I knew perfectly well. I was thinking of the separation from my mother, my loved ones, thinking that it was unlikely I would soon find myself at their home or in Moscow, and about how my hitherto tragic life would end.
I imagined heroic scenes where I would become the victim of an “accidental” murder, like some Gandhi, which had happened to many other public figures, monks, and saints. I had, of course, soon decided to add myself to their ranks. These images of a tragic death would not leave me.

Suddenly Yanis—as I said, he was a local Casanova, proud of it—again showed an unusual sensitivity or intuition, though he was clearly tired after his shift; he was finishing up his work and apparently waiting for someone to replace him… Suddenly, as if reading my thoughts, he uttered a phrase that left me bewildered: “Everyone has their own cross,” he said, looking at me sympathetically, “or how do you say it in English?” he laughed. To this, I could not help but laugh too, out of surprise that it was from his lips… I answered him with an even heavier, more ponderous rhetoric about what it is like for a man to die for no reason at all, and he suddenly, as if he had sensed my thoughts again, cut in just as confidently and calmly: “But that is beautiful—to die for what you believe in! Much better than just living for nothing”—and he smiled again, openly, cordially, and even fatherly. It felt like we were playing poker, and I was losing, while he covered everything with some skillful and inspired card.

And where did he even get such a wise outlook (I hadn’t noticed that in him before), I wondered; to this, he turned away lightly, as if he were a man with a sense of a completed task or a small victorious battle, and added quietly, “It happens to me.”

I have heard this phrase about the cross more than once from different people… and I have thought a lot about what it means. Many times people have said something to me that was, at that very moment, important, necessary…

How did they know? Intuition? Or is it a kind of insight granted to us who are in special spiritual proximity to one another? I think it is He, the Holy Spirit; for people who have fallen away from Him and are distant are rarely capable of playing the necessary role in the lives of others, let alone their own. Bright people, as a rule, are talented in these matters, and Yanis—he regularly says something so necessary, supporting the people around him: often without even realizing it himself.

She came flying toward me and was very, very happy when she saw me: “I was just hoping I’d run into you! Saint John Cassian

He took the name John, in all likelihood, in memory of his teacher—the famous theologian John Chrysostom. From childhood, in his family, the future John received the foundations of Christian upbringing. Later, he studied classical philosophy and rhetoric; in short, he was not deprived of knowledge or the attention of his kin. He undertook a pilgrimage to Palestine with another man, Germanus, where he decided to renounce the world. Having mastered the basics of askēsis (in translation from Greek, *askēsis* means exercise), he and his friend decided to set off for Egypt. They traveled by sea and desert to the monastery of the famous Abba Pinufius, where they happened to meet monks living on hills among salt lakes (Pinufius lived near the others in a small cell). They ended up in Diolcus, where they also conversed with wise fathers. In conversing with the ascetics, Germanus and John gathered wisdom from the monks, sought counsel, and learned various things. They were fortunate to meet and learn from such monks as Paphnutius, Moses, and others known today.

While staying there, John exhausted himself with fasting and physical labor, and they would gather in the church for services—there, they all exercised in theology together. After ten years, he had grown spiritually and gained knowledge and spirit from experienced Fathers and pilgrims. In the year 399, unrest arose in Egypt, caused by the teaching of the Anthropomorphites—heretics who believed that God possessed a body similar to man’s. Archbishop Theophilus of Alexandria condemned this as strictly heretical knowledge. He was supported by Abba Paphnutius and a multitude of other desert dwellers.

The dissatisfied followers of the Anthropomorphites managed to convince Theophilus to move away from the Origenist teachings—the teachings of the Christian Origen, who lived and died a martyr’s death in the third century. Consequently, the monks were forced to seek shelter and support in other lands. Some Origenists found protection in the person of the head of the Constantinopolitan Church, Saint John Chrysostom.

When Saint John Chrysostom was condemned and exiled, the two friends were sent with a message to the West—to the Roman Bishop Innocent I. There, during his 12-year service, John Cassian was raised to the priesthood and even received the position of assistant to the Roman Bishop. There, in all likelihood, he became acquainted with Pope Leo the Great.

In 415, driven by a desire for solitude, John Cassian found himself in Southern Gaul (today this is the city of Marseille); there, he befriended the local bishop and subsequently established two monasteries, one of which—a men’s monastery—he headed himself. His fame as a spiritual guide soon spread throughout Southern Gaul, far beyond the borders of Massalia. At the request of local bishops, Father John compiled a set of rules for cenobitic monasteries, drawing upon his many years of experience living in a community in Egypt.

He also authored a number of significant theological treatises, including 'On the Incarnation of the Lord' and, slightly earlier, the 'Conferences.' It is believed that John Cassian passed away in the year 435 and was laid to rest in the community of Saint Victor.

Once, a young boy asked the future St. Christopher—then known as Reprobus, a man of extraordinary stature believed to have the face of a dog—to carry him across a river. Mid-stream, Christopher felt an unbearable weight, as if he were holding the entire world. It turned out that on his shoulder he bore not only the world, but its Creator—Christ Himself, having appeared to the future saint as a young child. Seized with terror that he would fail to bear the boy and that both would surely drown, Christopher was comforted when the child revealed who He was and what Christopher was carrying: the burdens of the world. Right there, in the very river they were crossing, Jesus baptized Reprobus, bestowing upon him the new name 'Christopher,' which means 'Christ-bearer.'

Before even exiting the river, the child instructed Christopher to thrust his staff into the earth, where it miraculously blossomed into a fruit-bearing tree. Through this, many were brought to the faith.

There are many legends of St. Christopher. Indeed, tradition holds that he was of fearsome appearance; historical documents confirm he was captured by the Romans during battle in Marmarica and was frequently subjected to brutal beatings. Through his deep and constant desire to follow Christ, the saint strove never to let his words or deeds turn to anger, accepting all things with humility.

Mythological lore suggests the martyr possessed the head of a dog; however, a later version common in Cyprus posits that he was, in fact, very handsome and, seeking to avoid temptation, prayed for God to take away his beauty, whereupon he took on a dog-like appearance. From this, perhaps, arose the myth of a holy man with the head of a fierce hound.

Suffering followed Reprobus on his path. Throughout his life, he diligently rebuked those who persecuted Christians. The local governor, the Roman Emperor Decius Trajan, was enraged by the miracle of the flowering tree, among the other wonders attributed to Reprobus, and cast him into prison. In 250, the martyr died in Lycia after numerous tortures, finally being beheaded by the sword. Throughout his ordeals—being thrown into a well and forced to wear a tunic of red-hot copper—he never renounced himself or his faith in the Child and God.

For a long time, the saint’s relics were kept in Constantinople before being transported to the island of Rab in Croatia; today, one of the island's grandest medieval fortresses bears his name. In the Catholic tradition, Christopher is honored as one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, alongside St. Panteleimon, and as the patron saint of travelers, much like St. Nicholas the Wonderworker.

Saint Spyridon

From childhood, St. Spyridon emulated the righteous men of the Old Testament—David, Jacob, and Abraham—tending sheep and living a pure, God-pleasing life. Later, he became the father of a large family. Unusually kind-hearted, St. Spyridon attracted many homeless and wanderers who found refuge in his person and shelter and sustenance in his home. For his obedience, the Lord endowed the future saint with the gifts of clairvoyance and healing.

After his wife passed away, St. Spyridon was chosen as Bishop of Tremithus during the reign of Constantine the Great (324–337). He continued to combine his pastoral ministry with works of mercy. In 325, St. Spyridon participated in the affairs of the famous First Ecumenical Council.

There, he diligently challenged the opinion of a Greek philosopher who, following the Alexandrian priest Arius (the 'Arian heresy'), argued that Christ was not the eternally begotten Son of God the Father, but merely a supreme creature. Upon hearing the saint's clear speech, the opponent of Christianity became its zealous defender and received Baptism.

Legend says that at that same Council, St. Spyridon took a brick in his hands to demonstrate the unity of the Holy Trinity; fire instantly flared from it, water flowed down, and only the clay remained. 'Look, three elements, but one brick,' the saint declared, 'so it is in the Most Holy Trinity—Three Persons, yet one Godhead.' Thus he stood against Arianism in favor of the divine nature of Christ.

St. Spyridon often showed strictness—at his command, a merciless grain merchant was punished to save the local villagers from hunger and poverty. When a long drought and famine gripped Cyprus, intense, lasting rains fell at the saint’s prayer, and the disaster ceased.

When St. Spyridon set out to save a friend unjustly imprisoned and sentenced to death, his path was blocked by a raging torrent. Remembering the story of Joshua crossing the swollen Jordan, the saint prayed to God, and the waters parted. The judge, upon hearing of the miracle, released the innocent prisoner.

Many other wonders were performed by St. Spyridon. For instance, once during a service, the oil was running low, but the Lord comforted him, and the lamp filled itself again. Another time, when Spyridon entered an empty church to begin a service, he proclaimed, 'Peace be to all,' to which a multitude of voices from above responded, 'And to thy spirit!' The choir was sweeter than any human song. It was as if angels were participating in the service, repeating 'Lord, have mercy' at every litany. People nearby heard this, but when they reached the edge of the church, they saw nothing to explain the suddenly vanished heavenly singing that had so delighted their hearts. They were astounded.

The saint healed many, including the gravely ill Emperor Constantius, and once spoke to his own recently deceased daughter, already prepared for burial. A woman once came to him with a dead child in her arms; having prayed, the saint restored the infant to life, causing the mother, perhaps from shock, to fall down dead herself. It is said that by the power of his prayer, the saint brought her back to life as well.

Once, thieves attempted to steal St. Spyridon’s sheep but found themselves bound by an invisible force. When the saint came to the flock in the morning and found the robbers tied, he untied them and urged them to abandon their unlawful path. Finally, having prayed, he gifted each of them a sheep and gently added, 'So that your vigil may not be in vain.' They departed the fold.

As a bishop, the saint was an example to his flock: he strictly observed the liturgical order and was zealous in maintaining the integrity of Holy Scripture, rebuking priests who quoted it or other God-inspired books inaccurately.

The life of St. Spyridon is striking for its simplicity and the power of the miracles granted to him by God. By his words, the dead were awakened and the elements tamed. It is also known that when the Patriarch summoned a Council in Alexandria to destroy all idols and pagan temples, they managed, through prayer, to shatter all save one, which, by revelation to the holy Patriarch, could only be destroyed by St. Spyridon of Tremithus. When summoned to the Council, he boarded a ship, and as soon as he stepped onto land, the idol in Alexandria fell and crumbled into dust, together with all the altars. By this, he signaled his arrival to the Patriarch and the bishops.
