The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste

'He that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.'
John 11:25

In 313, St. Constantine the Great issued a decree granting Christians freedom of religion and equal rights with pagans. But his co-ruler Licinius was a staunch pagan and decided to eradicate Christianity in his portion of the empire. Preparing for war against Constantine, and fearing betrayal, Licinius decided to purge his army of Christians.

At that time, in the Armenian city of Sebaste, one of the commanders was Agricolaus, a zealous proponent of paganism. Under his command was a troop of forty Cappadocians, brave warriors who had emerged victorious from many battles. All of them were Christians. When the soldiers refused to sacrifice to the pagan gods, Agricolaus cast them into prison. The warriors devoted themselves to fervent prayer and one night heard a voice: 'He who endures to the end, the same shall be saved.'

The next morning, the soldiers were brought again before Agricolaus. This time, the pagan resorted to flattery. He praised their courage, youth, and strength and again urged them to renounce Christ to earn honor and the Emperor's favor. Upon hearing their refusal, Agricolaus ordered them to be shackled. However, the eldest of them, Quirion, said: 'The Emperor did not give you the right to place chains upon us.' Agricolaus, discomfited, ordered the soldiers to be taken back to prison without chains.

Seven days later, the noble official Lysias arrived in Sebaste and held a trial. The saints answered firmly: 'Take not only our military rank, but our lives; for us, there is nothing more precious than Christ God.' Lysias then ordered them to be stoned. But the stones flew wide of the mark; a stone thrown by Lysias hit Agricolaus in the face. The tormentors realized the saints were guarded by an invisible power. That night in prison, the warriors prayed and again heard the Lord’s comforting voice: 'He that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live. Be bold and fear not, for you shall receive incorruptible crowns.'

The next day, the interrogation by the torturer was repeated, yet the warriors remained unyielding.

It was winter, and the frost was intense. The holy warriors were stripped, led to a lake near the city, and left under guard on the ice for the entire night. To break their will, a warm bath was prepared on the nearby shore. In the first hour of the night, when the cold became unbearable, one warrior could not hold out and ran toward the bath, but no sooner had he crossed the threshold than he dropped dead. In the third hour of the night, the Lord sent relief: suddenly it became light, the ice melted, and the water became warm. All the guards were asleep, save one named Aglaius. Looking at the lake, he saw a bright crown hovering over each martyr’s head. Aglaius counted thirty-nine crowns and realized that the soldier who had fled had lost his. Then Aglaius awakened the other guards, stripped off his clothes, and cried, 'I am a Christian too!' and joined the martyrs. Standing in the water, he prayed: 'Lord God, I believe in Thee, in Whom these soldiers believe. Join me to them, that I may be worthy to suffer with Thy servants.'

In the morning, the tormentors were amazed to see that the martyrs were alive and their guard Aglaius was glorifying Christ with them. Then the warriors were led from the water and their legs were broken. During this agonizing execution, the mother of the youngest, Melito, urged her son not to fear and to endure to the end. The bodies were placed on carts to be burned. Young Melito was still breathing, so he was left on the ground. His mother then picked up her son and carried him on her shoulders, following the cart. When Melito breathed his last, she placed him on the cart beside the bodies of his holy companions. Their bodies were burned, and their charred bones thrown into the water, so that Christians could not collect them.

Three days later, the martyrs appeared in a dream to the blessed Peter, Bishop of Sebaste, and commanded him to bury their remains. The bishop and several clerics gathered the remains of the glorious martyrs by night and buried them with honor.

Fri, 16 Mar. 18
The monastery was under construction—a whole team of craftsmen was working there. The abbot of the Monastery of St. Seraphim of Sarov seemed an attentive mentor, yet deeply immersed in his own cares. He painted icons of astonishing beauty; he had painted the entire altar, not to mention other churches in Cyprus to which he had also contributed. He was exceptionally focused and answered any of my queries or desires to talk with a curt refusal—'Go work,' he’d say. And I would obediently head out to the fields, or to the bulldozers... There, a longtime friend of the abbot, of French origin, who was very intelligent and spoke English beautifully, was waiting for me.

He gave me tasks, as he was in charge of all the construction work, and in the intervals, we discussed changes in society and other controversial topics. He had many ideas of his own—that Freud with his analysis was no longer relevant, that people and society had changed, and now, perhaps, we could create ourselves and each other from whatever parts we were given; building and training our bodies, training our reason, modeling our minds. Not everything he told me was close to my heart, but I listened carefully; surely, it cannot be that all previous knowledge has disappeared into obsolescence! Now, perhaps, I would agree with him on everything. Nevertheless, I was particularly grateful for one thing he taught me—he showed me how important it is, without fearing difficulty, to engage in physical labor, alternating one task with another... And how necessary it is to surrender oneself completely to the process; if you are clearing stones, then think only of them; if you are riding the crane lift to trim the branches of dead trees, then live and breathe that very moment, surveying the world around you from the heights. There, at the height of those branches, everything seems different—nature breathes, speaks to you, and the scent of the boughs is almost intoxicating. I am grateful to him for these lessons... Regarding psychology and post-modernism, we shall all understand soon enough—until then, it is better to refrain from loud proclamations about the irreversibility of change and simply live, like these people building yet another, yet somehow unique, monastery.


Fri, 16 Mar 18
In the presence of the abbot’s mother, it was surprisingly warm and cozy, and the food she prepared for all the monastery workers felt wonderfully homemade and delicious. I walked into the hut and immediately felt as if I had ended up somewhere at a summer cottage, perhaps near Moscow, where I once grew up, and everything that followed—the food, the conversation—seemed torn from my past life and brought directly here as an unexpected gift. Greenery was visible all around, almost like the birch trees at our dacha... On the wooden table sat a steaming pot of what seemed to be mushroom soup, and my hands were warmed by a mug of homemade green tea. For the first time in Cyprus, I felt completely rested, as if at home. It is hard to convey how much this can mean when you have been traveling for a long time without stopping and cannot find your place. It seems the Lord sent this to me as a celebration, a release for my journey, and I knew that even though it was not infinite—both the meal and this conversation would inevitably end soon—but while this miracle was here, I had to soak in every moment, every second, and every view from the window, which, like this moment, would likely never be repeated. There will be something else, perhaps another release! And I think we have something to wait for; after all, you never know behind which corner such an unexpected and wonderful gift hides—healing and warming the heart, as if erasing the traces of all previous difficulties or sometimes agonizing failures.

It seemed to me that the abbot was overly harsh, even though I saw him as a deeply thoughtful man. It always surprised me when church people, who appeared profound, exhibited temper or misplaced principle in matters that could have been handled differently. On one hand, soft as butter; on the other, short-tempered, nitpicking, almost grumbling. And in such cases, I always asked myself: if God is love, should not softness and warmth toward another human being be before all our needs, views, and rituals? Is this not our gauge of how close we are to the Kingdom of Heaven? This, as I observed during my trip, is the main thing that blocks people’s path to the Church. They, too, having encountered such a manifestation once, do not understand—if this is a representative of the Church, is it worth my going there? Nevertheless, at the end of my difficult week of labor, working on equal terms with all the workers in this monastery, with its long and tireless services, the father saw me off with such warmth that I was left with a pleasant aftertaste, along with his blessings.

Vera, a friend from Moscow, sent me SMS messages, each one like a precious piece of guidance. Vera's messages were about the path, about how important it is to stick to it. This poem, which began the irreversible process of change, became the foundation for future growth.

It is extremely important for the soul to be constantly at work. I learned this, on one hand, from Russian poetry, which has often proclaimed this simple thought ('do not let your soul be lazy, so as not to grind water in a mortar,' Zabolotsky), and on the other, at the Monastery of St. Seraphim of Sarov. I realized that clearing a pile of stones with a shovel is no simple task—it requires technical skill and an active mind; it has a need for method, much like philosophy. You need to know how to hold the shovel properly so it slides along the surface of the ground, scooping up heavy stones without much effort or strain; you need to be resilient and suppress the urge to whine when you are tired; finally, you need to learn to go to the end and not give up, because everyone has their own share—their own task—and no one will do it for you. Any intellectual work must be alternated with activity, and activity that is maximally vigorous. You need to drop everything when you feel a little tired or exhausted—when the flight is over—and immediately, lightning-fast, tune into a physical mode and do something that requires your effort. Believe me, there is no better medicine for adversity! Especially when it feels like there is no way out. Like my friends from the monastery, the Frenchman and another acquaintance who chose the path of grueling physical labor despite their education, I found the skill of living this way useful. My second acquaintance, a philosophy teacher from Greece, came to the monastery specifically for such a change. We worked together, talking the whole time about how physical labor becomes addictive and isn't easy to simply quit... In strong physical shape himself, he never tired of repeating: 'Once you start living like this, it’s not so easy to stop. Physical exertion is like doping.'

In one place, opposite the Faneromeni church, another person helped me once. He gave me twenty euros, which was enough for a night in a nearby hotel, and just cheered me up a bit. Siemes owns a small cafe or club—people with piercings and tattoos hang out there; there are graffiti images of naked women on the walls. Siemes himself looks civilized, goes to church, and, according to his son, is a great spiritual authority in his circle; apparently, he has seen a lot and gained experience. Now he hardly appears in the cafe, though I managed to catch him for a minute, and the younger generation runs everything. There I met a waiter I really liked—who is Muslim by origin, although his mother is Christian, and he was raised as a Christian in his childhood. He told me about his warm memories of his childhood around the church, and about how he is no longer drawn to the church because it all seems excessive to him; he clearly needs some direction, as it seemed to me, and is now thinking about what to do next. The guy's eyes burned, unlike many others, and he—during our private conversation over beer—said one key phrase that I felt distinguished him from those around him; he said it with a slight mockery, but firm as flint: 'I don't care what I do—I'm not afraid of work.' And then I realized that behind that phrase lay much more courage than just a lack of fear of work—he was not afraid of life, in all its unexpected manifestations, and was ready, despite childhood hurts, to reconsider any of his ideas and views if life posed such a question. And in this lay his directness and strength, making him self-sufficient and firmly on his feet. He finished his cigarette, smiled at the girls at the next table, and rushed back to his work—with a smile never leaving his face and with a readiness to meet something new.

***

I heard the ringing of bells, which sounded bright. I was surprised that the ringing of bells could sound so joyful! It seems they were playing something popular from Christmas music; at least, that is how the ringing sounded to me... So I went inside; it was the Cathedral of St. Anne. What I saw inside also pleased me—as happens in a Catholic church, the altar was entirely open, and the parishioners were just about to take communion. The priest (though one increasingly wants to call him 'pastor') was cheerful and joyful, and he delivered his sermon loudly and briskly. It seemed to me quite interesting—to take communion in such a cheerful atmosphere, to the sound of bright, joyful bells! Nevertheless, I realized then that I would not want to be a parishioner of such a church, that for me, the mystical mystery, the contemplative nature of Eastern Orthodoxy, is precious, and I would not want to leave it. After all, there really is something to it: the closed, mysterious altar, where entry to the uninitiated is, as a rule, forbidden... In the tradition of magic.

This does not mean at all that our bells could not sometimes play a slightly more joyful, ringing melody, from time to time emerging from the pensive, yet, to me, valuable introspection. However, every parish must, I think, decide this for itself... But if it were not for this music, which rang out across our whole district, reminding me in its notes of our 'In the forest, a Christmas tree was born,' I would not have known about this church and would not have gone inside.

I grew very fond of the Cathedral (Holy Transfiguration of Christ), which was blessed in the early twentieth century by St. Tikhon, Patriarch of Moscow. A great ascetic who traveled the world over, he founded a multitude of churches and parishes, particularly throughout North America.

What unites everyone in this temple is a spirit of friendliness, openness to one another, and fellowship. For instance, the bell-ringer—who, due to the unusual placement of the cathedral’s bells, is often obliged to stand right by the entrance—embraces everyone with incredible warmth and openness, regardless of their appearance, culture, or even, I believe, their faith. At the door, no one will ask if you know the ecclesiastical rules or if you have completed the prescribed readings before Communion. Here, they will simply embrace you, ask how you are, where you come from, and how you happened to find your way here, then allow you to join in freely, in whatever capacity and measure of readiness you possess. The bells were a gift to the church from the last Russian Emperor—a direct donation from him to this specific American parish.

Because of its diversity, this motley and multifaceted parish has, in a way, lost that singular spirit we are accustomed to maintaining and preserving—and I think that is for the best! First, there is the fact that such American churches delight and surprise one with the variety of their parishioners: the different skin colors, manners, and appearances…

In the church garden, where there is an annex for meals and other community needs dedicated to a priest who has since passed (I believe he served there from 1986 until recently), there stands a tree split in two. It turned out that lightning had once struck it, cleaving it in half, leaving a gaping hollow where the trunk should be and robbing the tree of its life. When the moment came to fell it, the cleric (the very one in whose honor the building was named) suggested they pray first and perhaps delay the decision. Moreover, he hung a very beautiful icon within the hollow inside the tree and suggested they wait. After some time—by the following spring—the tree did indeed blossom as it once had, and has blossomed every year since, no worse than any other tree! It had seemed completely lifeless before; as I understand it, without the core of its trunk, it should have had virtually no chance. Nevertheless, it came to life, and the icon still hangs there, even though the priest has since left us.

A wonderful priest, serving there today, to whom I turned for help, told me in confession that for him, the primary spiritual authority is the text of the prayers. Since he became a priest, there has been no better teacher for him. And I like that detail—one can learn so much from these words.

***

I was climbing a staircase, and on every step, I saw a different story; perhaps it was a spiral staircase. I saw my whole life before my eyes, as if from a bird’s-eye view.
As I ascended, I saw different clouds, wispy ones, and suddenly I understood that everything is entirely different. You, your fears and limitations, your anxieties. And, of course, the interpretations of your past—they appear quite different from this step! For you realize that you have grown by an entire step, which means your past interpretations and perspectives are no longer a fit. 'Please, send me a new interpretation... from the spiral staircase, renewed and, ideally, true,' and God, of course, does not leave such a request unheard, for He does not send a stone to one who asks for bread.

But before moving to the next step, I had to be certain of the following: that I had overcome the fears that stood out most sharply while I stood on the previous step. That I am no longer afraid! And those dangers, however monstrous they may have seemed before, are no longer dangerous at all, and you will be glad to accept them if it be the Lord’s will.

Moreover, you will be prepared, with the ease of a supple acrobat, to leap through these difficulties into the very depths of what you feared most, neutralizing the problem by seeing it, finding it, and looking into its heart. Only then will you find yourself free. Only then will you reach that step on the staircase from which you can see everything—just as it is, but in due time, not a moment sooner. Only then will you draw near to your own authentic life. And until then, rest assured—this staircase will end, and everything will be quite unlike what you expected…
***

There were many wonderful encounters, too. Once, our family friend, almost a relative, Igor, told me about his great love. Or rather, about how in every man's life there is a woman, an image he idolizes above all else, and every time he meets such a woman, he goes mad for her, plunging into the abyss. He believed he was doomed to this.
This feeling, alas, exerts a powerful influence on a man, until he learns to reconcile with this archetype in his relationships.

***

'To be in the present, neither racing into the future nor lagging in the past—this is ascetic labor. <...> I once said that "cunning" is a distortion. It is when your path turns into a crooked bow. But it is truly very difficult to walk in a straight line; it seems almost impossible. However, do you know how one can walk not in a straight line, yet without cunning? In small, straight segments. A circle, on a small enough arc, is near to a straight line.' – Fr. Sergii Ovsyannikov wrote this about time and space, and I could not write it better.

***

Once, I found myself in my beloved St. John the Forerunner Monastery…

Father Bartholomew gave me a couple of sound pieces of advice. One went: 'failure to plan is failure to achieve' (which is, undoubtedly, true in some respects… although I, for one, love to break away and fly); and another (a well-known quote): 'traditionalism is the dead faith of the living, while tradition is the living faith of the dead'—this I liked very much.

He also said that the Church should judge the secular world for its misuse of the word 'love.' After all, this word is not about liking something, but about what another person finds good and agreeable to their soul. 'Love,' he said, 'is about the other person, not about our ego.'

***
We are like batteries, he said, and we expend the strength given to us by God. Energy for service, for serving beauty. If it is not used, it is a disaster. 'Energy is love.' 'When salt loses its savor, it becomes poison'—I remembered from BG. The reverse force, from an unused battery dissolving within and turned against us, he believed, is effectively what depression is.

'Let prayer become your narcotic!' he repeated. Father Sophrony, the founder of the monastery, once said that we experience dependence on whatever we find solace in—the very thing that is meant to help us. Even prayer ropes can be no less of a dependence, Fr. Bartholomew said to me in passing.
And finally: 'Love could not exist on any other planet, in any way. It shouldn't even be here, on Earth… We must marvel at this miracle. Every day.'
Then we parted ways.

***

In the monastery bookstore, I began talking about my journey with the nun selling the books. She asked about my spiritual father—I said he was far away... 'You need someone to guide you,' she answered kindly. 'And furthermore,' she added, 'it is very important to advance in faith, but one must do so with humility.' She said this because I had complained to her that when one breaks through to God, one often feels a sense of danger, as if a gatekeeper stands at every door. Often, he manifests as some sort of temptation, and, yes, as a rule, these are expressed precisely in pride: 'It cannot be otherwise!', 'I must do this!', or something similar; but at the center, there is always one's own 'I.' And so, perhaps that is why she spoke to me of humility, and I know from experience that nothing else can save. These are the very narrow gates. I say this not because I am myself very humble, but precisely because I know how, like magic, it helps one to overcome paths that are at times impassable.

Next, I met an old acquaintance of mine, a relative of Fr. Sophrony, Father Nikolai. Once, he participated in a meeting where I and a fellow student were present; there, he spoke to the whole room about marital fidelity. Despite the subject and angle, which I found unsuccessful, we became friends, and in 2012, he gave me a prayer rope that has become a talisman for me.

I have spent much time thinking about the nature of sin—about whether it can be overcome, whether the multitude of one’s own thoughts can be conquered. I believe it is possible, but the trouble is that they do not retreat so easily; one must search with particular diligence for approaches, sometimes far removed from tradition, to grapple with oneself and with them (with these impulses and thoughts). One must sometimes seek one’s own methods, capable—in addition to the wisdom of tradition—of keeping this boat, wavering upon the waves, afloat. How difficult this is! Oh, if only there were one ready-made way to defeat them all, once and for all! There is only the path itself and the faith that can hold us upon it, even when all seems lost. And there is an inner intuition capable of whispering: 'This is not the way. Be careful, do not step there.' It is almost like that very notched, chipped staircase in Brodsky’s poetry. Yet everything is relative and requires a particularly careful, internal working-out… Only in this way can one hold on and not perish, having found one’s own method.

***

Once, at a service, I met a choir director—a massive man with tattoos, a biker. I kept wondering, how, how will I know what my calling is?—this theme swirled in my head. And then, taking me aside after the service, he said suddenly: 'You won’t understand this now, but... Do you want to know what to do? One day you will look back and see that you have been doing exactly what you have been doing your whole life—and that was your calling.' It seems we spend our whole lives doing the one thing, stubbornly searching the corners for something we call a 'calling,' when it is already here, right beside us.

***
In England, a story occurred involving a girl from Sri Lanka; this time, I was waiting for a taxi. The girl was leaving the hospital where my sister had been admitted. It was night. I turned to this beautiful girl and, in a sudden leap of trust, asked if she knew of a good taxi firm. I didn't want to Google it. 'Happy Cabs,' she replied at once.

The car was surprisingly good, and the name carried a sense of joy. Ever since, for several years, we used only Happy Cabs, thanks to that girl at the bus stop. The main thing is sometimes to catch a moment of chance and not bury one’s head in the solitude of a mobile phone.

Still, it is good when you are doing precisely your own work—one feels very clearly that this is so, that you are on 'the path' and are dying, as it were, with Christ; my dear older friend, a philosopher, wrote well about this, citing the words of Fr. Sophrony: 'One cannot live with Christ; one can only die with Him.'

***

There is a song by the band Bright Eyes. The renowned songwriter and bard Conor Oberst says in it: 'Everything it must belong somewhere'—this refrain is repeated many times. Pencils sit organically in a pencil case, matches in a matchbox: they are in their proper place.

'Cause everything it must belong somewhere
Just like the gold around her finger or the silver in his hair
Yeah, everything it must belong somewhere
I know that now, that’s why I’m staying here
Oh, I know that now, that’s why I’m staying here'

—this is an inspiration from my childhood. Conor Oberst, by the way, has many Christmas songs. Christmas compositions can also be found in the works of Aimee Mann, Leonard Cohen, and Nick Cave.

Every person has 'their own' place, and one should strive, all one’s life, to discover this cherished shell. 'I know that now, that’s why I’m staying here,' the song says. This illusion of adventure and searching is mentioned in the tale of the girl from the Land of Oz, with her phrase, 'I never want to go searching for myself beyond my backyard.' *The Wonderful Wizard of Oz* is a very wise fairy tale.
IN RUSSIA
—Come down to see me, —said Marianna, my beloved neighbor.

Marianna once played the lead role in the film *The Stationmaster*. I went down to the fifth floor. She would often, out of the kindness of her heart, feed me soup, or might pour me a glass if there was an occasion, or treat me to something sweet. But this time was special—on the table, she had prepared fresh cottage cheese with strawberries, sour cream, and sugar. A cozy kitchen, with a board covered in notes and photographs (looking at me from it was, for instance, BG—a friend of Marianna’s), faces important to her, fresh, glistening strawberries, farm-fresh sour cream from our local parish church. But with her, things are never simply 'just so.' Marianna began to talk to me about something:

'Perhaps everything will be alright.' And then, coaxingly, as if she had called me over for this very reason: 'Would you ever want to film a movie about Christ?' The strawberries were stunning. Then Marianna took some *solyanka* from the fridge, along with beautifully arranged pickles... And indeed, everything was alright. Very good, even.

She had somehow sensed this mood of mine. It embedded itself in my memory for a long time—'everything will be alright'...

Do you remember, in Kazakov’s film *The Shadow, or Perhaps Everything Will Work Out*, the phrase was spoken: 'if the little one smiles, perhaps everything will work out.'

***

I returned to Moscow on New Year’s Eve (my mother had said, 'Do it, it will be beautiful'); I was traveling from Wales, literally like a diver on his last minute of oxygen, having scrambled to buy a bus ticket, then a plane ticket—buying the ticket while already on the bus—so difficult was it to decide. I remember sitting in the airport before departure, watching the minutes tick by... Should I decide to go, or should I stay after all? For when I had left, my confessor had firmly told me to leave and not return for as long as possible...

By a miracle, I made it—not only to the plane, which I was tempted to cancel until the very moment of boarding, but also to a New Year’s celebration at a friend’s dacha. It so happened that my trip to Cyprus had been during the New Year; I was alone then. My return to Moscow also happened on New Year’s. Quite by chance, but now, almost by tradition.

We drank champagne, and I went off to my friends’ dacha (also a tradition). I had been away from home for two years, or perhaps six months—I had left with the feeling of never coming back. Why? What tasks was I meant to solve? Or is life merely one continuous jolt, devoid of any goal?

***

Later, Marianna and I often met on the bench 'in the neighborhood,' eating ice cream—I would run for it, picking out bars that hadn't melted, from the bottom of a perpetually broken freezer in the local shop—smoking thin cigarettes, talking about other neighbors, the weather, and about life—always about it!—what did we not converse about?

I remember how Marianna, among other things, told me about cinema during an evening stroll: 'Cinema, Yasha, is a visual art. Night, street, streetlamp, pharmacy.'—she pointed to the surrounding night and the streetlamp. It is no wonder she is a film critic from the House of Cinema, and a very wise, sensitive person.

While we ate our ice cream, our friend, a well-known professor, would often emerge from around the corner—greeting us with a sparkle in his eye and a touch of bravado, tossing out some sharp question, again about football or a remark aimed at the authorities. We walked along the boulevard. He walked that path every day.

The time came to apply for reinstatement at GITIS. Our dean was an expressive, open man. Yet in Russia, a dean’s office is always a parliament of sorts. Just as they were about to deny my reinstatement, HE appeared—the dean himself—in high spirits. I approached Timofey Ivanovich, and with the effortless grace of a magician, he snatched the paperwork from one of his subordinate Moirai, asking no questions other than, “What have we here?” He plucked it from their hands as if performing a sleight of hand, and signed. With a deft stroke, he crossed something out, raised the document high with his elbow like a conductor, handed it to me with elegant flair, and hurried on. Thus, against the deanery’s discontent, I was reinstated in my studies.
I also needed the signature of my senior lecturer, Maria Vitalievna. She was the one who had admitted me to GITIS long ago, but she was now moonlighting at another institute.

When we met in the back alleys of that little-known Moscow theater institute, Maria Vitalievna was sitting in the courtyard, smoking nervously between lectures. She wore a hat. Everything was wreathed in smoke. Timofey Ivanovich had already told her about me... She said, “Here, a gift—take your diploma!” and handed me my grade book, complete with the missing subject and a flourish on the appropriate line.
It was an incredibly lucky turn of events, for by leaving for Cyprus, I had effectively severed all ties with the university.

I did manage to persuade my Master to sign the grade book for the missed subject. He invited me to his home, where, among other things, he spoke of how one must write—in fragments, soldering them together. “You, Yasha, are not a director, but a screenwriter,” he remarked. Our primary sessions with Vladimir Vladimirovich Mirzoev were always cloaked in a veil of secrecy, and he rarely liked to let anyone into his rehearsals. “Better to busy yourself with something useful,” he would brush me off.

***

A friend in the theater’s literary department helped me arrange my internship.

I met with Madeleine—a friend of mine, an actress—in a café with wooden tables. Long ago, she had acted in a film on the set of which I worked, and in parallel, through a priest and his parish—the same one I attended—we became friends.

There, at that same church, were other parishioners from the theater: a young deacon who had studied with me at GITIS, and another altar server, the actor Ilya Lyubimov. Indeed, Father Andrey, who became the rector of the Church of St. Antipas in Moscow, is also from the Fomenko Theater. I remember Father Andrey descending the steps of the church toward me, arms wide open, greeting me with, “Yakov!” I was with my friend. I would bet anything that this was our very first meeting. I am still baffled as to how he knew my name. Before then, while in Wales, I had only read about him, but he could not possibly have known who I was.

We sat in a room with chairs or benches, one of the rehearsal halls. The Master spoke of synchronicity, and in essence, of what theology calls “chance.” He said that if a bird flies past the window, it is not by accident. If, at the moment we are thinking of something, a cat runs by, or in the neighboring rehearsal room someone starts singing an aria from Figaro in falsetto, these things, too, may be hints toward the resolution of a scene.

The Master was strict about many things. When we were rehearsing, he stopped a scene almost as soon as it had begun, after mere moments. Yes, we were playing poorly, and I expected to hear something about our interpretation.

“Casting error,” a gloomy voice sounded from the darkness. “The hero and heroine in this scene simply do not match energetically—it is the director’s mistake.” What were we to do? There were only a few people on the course suitable for the roles.

The Master strictly forbade me to write my own material for filming, explaining that it was a tautology—and tautology is a vice.

“Not always,” replied my spiritual father the next day during a walk from the metro… “Not every repetition is necessarily a tautology.”

I often called my spiritual father. “You are always calling at the wrong time!” he would respond affectionately. “Remember,” he told me as I stood at my window looking out at the view of southwestern nine-story blocks and high-rises, “that we see very little of what is given to us by our senses; everything else is a world constructed by the brain.” The high-rises loomed before me then like a scene from *Fight Club*; the curtains of our window on the ninth floor were thrown wide. Am I truly seeing all this, I thought, or are they about to crumble like dried paint, since I see only light and shadow? These are photons, they explained to me—photons of light.

Over time, a dialogue formed between the Master and my spiritual father, albeit indirectly.

“And how many scenes do you want to do for your diploma? Perhaps take fewer,” the priest advised.

Occasionally, when we met in a café, my spiritual father would lead me to the display case, where I could point a finger at a 'potato' pastry, and he would explain to me what that signified.

“So, why did I choose this? Why not something else?”

“No, Yasha, that is not intuition,” he explained. “It is coincidence. The fact that we are here is chance. But if you had said, upon a single glance at the pastry, that there was almond inside, and that you would dislike the pastry—that would be a different matter.”

Once, the Master pounded his fist on the table, severely rebuking me for disobedience. My spiritual father, by contrast, was gentle and always welcoming. The years have shown that both approaches have their value, though the latter is dearer to me.

At rehearsal, the Master pointed significantly at an object, implying it might come in handy for the hero at the right moment. We were staging Mozart at the time, and I had taken on the episode in the hall called the 'priestly temple.' I remember the Master’s assistant was horrified by our brooms, which we used as props. Then, one of the soloists was sweeping wood shavings from the floor, and the Master approached and tasked us with removing the brooms and replacing them with some elegant, sequined staff. Yes, in the theater, every trifle—especially one pertaining to ritual—plays a massive role.

I remember us arguing about whether postmodernism was only just beginning, whereas he insisted the era had ended and now something new would come—a sort of 'inflationary,' undeveloped thing, which is why the culture of our time is so primitive and reduced to banal pranks and TikToks; it simply hasn't ripened yet. We were just speaking of different things. I, of philosophy; he, of art.

In Russian, as in any language, terms sometimes lead to confusion—and while postmodernism has indeed come to an end, the post-modern (as a legacy of the philosophers of the 70s) is still in its prime (though there are debates as to whether it has arrived at all).
From time to time, Mirzoev would ask questions that were astonishing to me:

“Are you truly still stirred by this?” or “Do you imagine the images from books?” (— “No? Then you shall”) or “Ah, so that’s how it is for you?”—pointing to a non-trivial question about the perception of the world and the unique architecture of our brains...

I remember Marianna and me sitting by the entrance one day, talking, when she asked, 'Ah, so that’s how it is for you?' It happened the very next day. This question intrigues me greatly—it speaks to the fact that our own minds remain a mystery to us; each of us is individual in how we perceive things. What we see, what we think. That is why it is so interesting to live and describe one's sensations in this post-modern age. This word opens up an entire layer for exploration, and, as my comrade from the monastery used to say, perhaps the era of Freud has truly ended. The era of the phenomenon has begun. Indeed, it began with Kant.
I enjoyed this journey of discovery deep within myself.

The wonderful Mikhail Ugarov always taught the three-act structure of a work. 'Where the road leads,' he called the first act, the introduction into the narrative. During that period, I was diligently trying to understand dramaturgy and master cinema; I once dreamed—and sometimes still do—of capturing something from reality. For example, to record a young acquaintance of mine walking on an escalator in the subway, without interfering or stifling the freedom of that sincere moment. And then there was Mirzoev, who taught me just as I was about to film a scene from 'The Magic Flute' in the woods, that the camera should record what is interesting—as if it were already a finished scene. You can film on a phone; the camera is simply our eye, our observer. Let it observe.

I also had a spiritual father from childhood, my godfather and family mentor, who was also the founder of the Church of Antipas. I visited him once. That morning, I spent fifteen minutes in doubt, vacillating over whether to wear the watch my father had given me, and for some reason, I was too lazy to do so. I lived by such trivial actions. And so I arrived for a brief chat with Father Vladimir near the church. 'Life is a vale of suffering and sorrow,' he summarized, having listened to my agonizing thoughts. Then, he pulled back my sleeve with his finger to look at my wrist. He frowned slightly and, with a touch of humor and slight disappointment, remarked, 'Eh, I thought as much'… There was no watch on my wrist, and he had wanted to know the time.
Since then, if something from within urges me to wear a watch, I wear it.

***
'Kurwy!' Igor, our friend the professor and physician, would shout as he walked past the crows he was shooing away. I could never tell what we were discussing—football, a liberal president (a 'dwarf,' in Igor’s expression), the drug trade disguised as a neighborhood restaurant, or a universal conspiracy. We spoke of everything, but the conclusion was always unequivocal: 'Kurrry!' And then we would rejoice at the appearance of a film and theater actress who lived nearby. She would periodically run past toward her home, sometimes with her child. Her appearance was akin to a falling star—a sort of good omen.

Once, I was running with another box of food, freshly caught fish with lemon and cilantro. The box was in a bag. He saw it, asked where I was rushing to, and I answered. 'Well, that is sacred,' he approved. He was always Soviet, of the Brezhnev era, adorned with two medals—including one for mercy—a man forever in a shirt and with such military carriage. He would button his shirt to the very top and wear it with a puffed-up bravado. He called our traditional boulevard walks by their medical term: 'the motio'.

Igor was strict and shared mysterious cases from his life, stories of deaths from urological complications and stagnation in men like Napoleon, Peter the Great, or Bulgakov. A curious professor, he was lonely, yet often flew to Cyprus, where he maintained a practice. When I arrived from Cyprus—where we had managed to meet once in Paphos for a Cypriot coffee and football—he met me at the entrance by the mailboxes, turned, and whispered almost inaudibly, 'I haven’t told anyone about your trip to Cyprus. I understand that this information is not for public disclosure.' And truly, there was something secret about the whole adventure, just as he had sensed.

There he sits on the bench, as usual, on that very boulevard, wearing glasses and studying his phone and the news with trembling attention. Every time we met, he would reflect and inquire about the latest. Igor would evaluate the girls walking past us on the boulevard, praising and criticizing Merkel, football, and the entire world. He adored Bulgakov, especially his short story 'Morphine,' which he suggested I adapt for the stage. He scolded everyone, especially the pigeons and the vile crows.

Once, I found myself at his home to attend to something, and I remember as if it were today that Soviet look: the old wallpaper, those empty, dusty bachelor bottles in the corner. Shelves locked for years, untouched, filled with volumes of literary journals. He read, but above all, the preservation of these volumes was a kind of pride, an act of homage to the greats. He found these volumes in series, at flea markets or sales.

Igor Vasilievich loved Ekaterina Dashkova and Ivan Ivanovich (Shuvalov)—famous historical figures. We walked back and forth for hours; he boasted of his collected works, his medals (of which there were two or three), and the two urology textbooks he had authored (he was a hereditary doctor, having inherited his practice from his father, an academician). He never managed to publish the final volume of his textbook.

Together with Marianna and Igor, we would look at the picturesque sunsets, walking along the boulevard with its red embossed stripe down the middle, scouting out drug-dealing schemes near the church in a small cafe that served as a front, and talking about everything under the sun… Once, a criminal scheme was uncovered, investigated, and the cafe was torn down, even though we had often eaten there. One of us would thoughtfully assess the weather aloud—Marianna, Igor, or I—whomever was the first to dare break the mysterious silence. Calmly, as if observing a painting in a museum, we would discuss the sunset. Tintoretto and Veronese were Igor’s favorite painters… our conversation about Tintoretto’s art was the liveliest thread in the lessons he gave me over the years we spent side by side—two years, or, if we include the time since we met and the Cyprus period, three or four. Then, he—an agnostic, if not an atheist (though he unfailingly congratulated me on every holiday!)—would speak of Christ, His depictions, and Italian churches, effortlessly recalling all the names with care: 'This painting was there,' he would say with indescribable love and gravity, 'and this fresco…' It was his personal altar in the corner of his room, if you will, a sanctuary and a relief. When he pondered the mystery of Christ’s relationship with Mary Magdalene and the human nature of Christ (his various theories, as a urologist, were quite natural and understandable—he held simple views on the relations between the sexes)—it was then that his manner held so much love and recognition—toward Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the art that had left a living seal on his soul and memory. Thus, thanks to him, I began to penetrate the secrets of paintings myself, ever so slightly.

He was an elderly man of the Brezhnev era, of Soviet stock. I zealously judged the political analyst Valery Solovey and other insiders/public informants who seemed to pass off information as 'experts on the inner workings of the world.' I do not like people from the agencies, those close to power, no matter which side they turn out to be informants for. He, however, respected them greatly; they intrigued him.

Once, when Igor was preparing to explode with rage at an insult to his idols, Marianna came and broke us up. I naively kept suggesting to him, a man of a different era, Ekaterina Schulmann and others as an alternative. Many of his patients were connected to the agencies and special services, a fact he usually kept quiet.

Toward the end of his life, we were walking to the Admiral center, both in jeans. He was wearing jeans of a brand he was proud of, telling me the news. We always discussed brands of jeans. Or rather, no, we talked about much more. But that evening, there was the usual wind, yet also a slight chill in our rapport. I felt shy and yearned to use the informal 'ty,' sensing the gravity of the moment. However, we had already been communicating as equals for years… but I never said it, though I could have:

'And what brand are yours?'

'Wrangler. Though you, it seems, have others…'

'Yes. Probably, I don’t remember.'

That was how our last conversation sounded; I didn't risk the informal, and mumbled something between 'yours' (informal) and 'yours' (formal).

Two weeks later, I learned of his hospitalization. Soon after, someone suddenly rang the building's doorbell and announced his death. We didn't see each other again—I had last dropped him off at the entrance (he was walking up, tired, to his home) after that foolish conversation about jeans. I want to find a way to describe this period of my life through the lens of the church community. And not just one specific parish, though I primarily attended one particular church. Once, in church, I locked eyes with a monk. After the service, he approached me—it turned out he was a Russian speaker. We went for a walk, which accidentally stretched into eight hours. For long months I had been waiting for something, and suddenly, while praying, 'When, oh when will it get easier?', I heard, 'On Sunday.' I was lying on the bed when good news arrived, and at that very second, a swallow flew into the room. This is what was in the message from my sister: 'On Sunday in Tbilisi, an ensemble of medieval music is playing.'
The swallow darted through the window in a sudden burst and began circling right above my head, then slipped into the next room and vanished from sight.

“It will be a good concert…”

I look around, but the swallow is nowhere to be seen; it had fluttered out through the open casement windows, framed by hanging vines. At the concert, a very sweet-looking girl I had met only minutes before approached me and suggested we walk together.
I lingered, and, to my regret, I lost her.

A man leaned out of a window on Citia Square, holding a cigarette; he was wearing a green shirt and seemed quite tipsy. In a raspy, coughing voice, he asked for my lighter. Mine was a ridiculous thing with a “666” sticker on it. I apologized, saying I didn't understand, but then I caught on, took it out, and gave him a light. “I’m just sitting here…” he said, speaking in that familiar, booze-soaked bass, his speech stumbling. “And you’re walking by, and, you know,” he gestured with his finger toward my heavy backpack, which had already become a topic of conversation among my friends, “the thing is… life,” he continued, slowly searching for the right words, stumbling slightly, “this here—this is not life.”
“This is not *your* life,” he suddenly blurted out. I was taken aback.
He continued directly, as if he had suddenly sobered up:

“You’re out here fucking around (forgive me, but we’re brothers, aren't we!)” — he pointed toward the neighboring courtyard where my friend’s mother lived — “when you don't even need to be. Tell me, do you love anyone?”
“Yes,” I said (and besides, to say “no one” in response to such a question would have been improper). I was in love with a friend in Moscow, a married woman with two children.
“There,” he replied, squinting. “That’s where you need to be—with them. And whatever you do, don't lose the children.”
(I had no children… but she did.)

“So, do you understand me? Don't lose them for anything, or you'll be left with emptiness… you know? So be with them and the kids.” He reached out a fragile hand, with long fingers and a scattering of liver spots…
“Look at me,” he says suddenly, “I give sweets to the children—” he gestures toward the road— “who walk by here… and so, you are needed by them. You must be with them.”
And so, arms locked across the window frame, our hands joined ten times over, we parted after each pause in his speech—he still speaking of his readiness to help me in any way he could…
This man turned out to be from the local Russian church, and a month later, I learned he was gone.

“And don't forget to give them my regards,” he added with a radiant smile… as if looking into the future… perhaps implying my children and the lady I had not yet won—or perhaps my relatives in that house where I would stop by without real need, out of a silly habit of procrastinating.

Later that same day, I got off the bus a few stops early to walk, and suddenly noticed a charming little restaurant, with a small, lonely table standing by the road—white and carved. I received an invitation to sit from a Georgian stranger on the veranda. This was the second David I had met that day—a guide to the sites of Georgia. He spoke with me for two hours about his life… about women and loves. About the theater his daughter was involved in. Finally, after we compared all the countries and women and beer brands we both knew, he gave me his business card, took me to the hotel he deemed suitable, and later drove me home. ***

The men offered noble toasts to children, to the ancestors of ancestors, and to our churches, “for only in them,” they said, “is there a presence of the spirit, as they are built on high ground”—and they spoke of this with great pride, while praising Comrade Stalin. Suddenly, this modest guy, Todo, arrived. He looked directly and searchingly at me and said, raising his glass, “To our acquaintance?” Five minutes later, he drank to my health, as if sending me a blessing on my way—and finally, he uttered: “Let us drink to our faith.”
Not to wealth, nor to the spirits of ancestors. Faith, as the Apostle asserts, is the assurance of things unseen. That is the kind of faith.
In the end, my unassuming advisor assured me that we would meet again, and this, too, sounded prophetic. It was not a premonition, but a trust in an unseen yet tangible feeling.

I will forever remember that ancient, crooked house with its stools, overturned and frozen in that position. And the portraits of the Leader on every wall, intermingled with candles, cozily left in hidden corners among paperclips and plates, also adorned with his image.

Kosti’s mother sat sewing some sort of shirt over a rickety stool made of wooden slats; above her hung a portrait of Comrade Stalin, whom she so revered. Another day, I was playing the guitar. She sat nearby, cheering me on with the resolve of a gallant commander, a self-assured teacher, yet in a whisper, though firm: “Go on, louder.” “Don't be afraid, Yashenka.” “Louder.” She echoed me softly, insistently but firmly… come on. I began to sing louder, and that was when my long-forgotten, multifaceted voice suddenly broke through—at times high, at times low—the expansive voice I had lost…

She looked at me with the keen eye characteristic of her and ordered me to shave. “Like a son.” She said, “Such a beautiful face,” and spoke a Georgian phrase that was translated for me as: “You are such a handsome fellow, if you were a girl, you would have been stolen.” “You must, while you can, strive to keep yourself in shape, to maintain yourself.”

Another playful remark came from her over the phone through her son: “Come on now, learn to love Stalin, or I don’t know what I’ll do to you.” I, in turn, repeated the data to her about the murder of citizens, the figure of 18 million people. “What are those? At most 40 thousand, and they were all traitors and turncoats. He was simply weeding out unworthy elements…”
And I, in turn, told her about the nine hundred thousand of the clergy.

"Do you know what they were really like?" she dismissed me, waving her hand. "You criticize them yourself, after all." "He surely knew the inner workings of it all; he’s a seminarian himself," her son added.

When I arrived for lunch, she—with the wry smirk of an eighty-year-old woman possessing a sharp mind and keen awareness—tossed a white napkin onto my place setting. Recalling my dubious stance, she joked, "That’s not a napkin—that’s a provocation!" She laughed good-naturedly—she loved me, after all—and retreated to the far corner of the room.
And just like that, the tension dissolved.
She was truly kind, possessed a gift for support, and was both gentle and firm.

I shall remember that evening of guitar playing, when I discovered my own range. And I shall remember those white napkins. I remember her silhouette behind the fabric screen that led from the kitchen to the bedroom, weaving something on an old sewing machine. Just a silhouette, like something out of a film.

I found parallels with the Gospel in various texts and in Hollywood films. Lewis, for example, wrote about how the heroes of Narnia sometimes forgot what had happened to them, and how they miraculously found themselves in another world. A powerful invention, by the way.

Another feast. Suddenly, while they were speaking in Georgian, I noticed sympathetic sighs and sadness on their faces. Mourning, as if something terrible had happened.

In a world where technology strives to match the human, esoterica and 'insights' about the world in the spirit of 'interconnectedness' are becoming common sense; celebrities like Jim Carrey publish books about the construct of consciousness, and leftist intellectuals have raked through and absorbed Heidegger and Derrida. The youth have long since moved past what the church sometimes remains silent about. And it is time for psychologists not to get stuck in the past, but to seek new hypotheses and dialogues. How simple is it, really, to stop an unwanted thought? What does the feeling of déjà vu mean? What is faith, and does it influence the expectation of the future? What is gender, is the inclination toward one orientation or another actually predestined, and where is the data confirming this? Or are we truly, as it is fashionable to believe, a kind of construct—do whatever you want, since you are performative.

Why, standing before all these questions opened up by performative theory, are both doctors and writers still occupied with God knows what? My spiritual father set up a one-on-one meeting with me, about three times, at Jagannath (where for some reason important meetings always happened—for instance, later, with my mother). Zhenya was already treating me with intolerance. And so, one day, I arrived with my bags in hand, and, remembering the story of Metropolitan Anthony of Sourozh about his departure, I hoped that this was the very turning point—a decisive setting sail for somewhere... Into some enchanted world or a secret community. I imagined it as the next stage of 'enlightenment.' He met me as before, wearing headphones, and this time he was resolute (he was always resolute) and stern:

'Go home to your sister,' he said, 'don't even think about running off anywhere.' These words shook me up properly, and I returned to my sister's home. I packed my things, put them in a suitcase, and sat waiting for the next opportunity to leave Moscow.

I was invited to London for a birthday. The first thing I saw there, which seemed long familiar to me from previous, quite different stays, was a face on a red New Year's poster advertising a concert, hanging at a bus stop; the poster depicted none other than Boris Grebenshchikov, and listed those Indian songs and compositions he planned to perform.

As he was one of my favorite authors back in Russia, I felt compelled to take this occurrence as a sign of approval, a fair wind… Especially since I was nearly penniless, and the concert was for charity. To find myself suddenly amidst the posters of a beloved and long-sought artist, whom I had dreamed of seeing and hearing for so long. Naturally, I planned to attend, even though a trip to the outskirts of Manchester awaited me at the time. Oxxxymiron also echoed frequently in my ears.

At the concert, I was greeted from the stage by strange chants, which turned out to be part of his program. It was all taking place in an old Anglican church.

Then BG himself took the stage, which brought me immense joy. I had to catch a train; I knew roughly when I would need to dash, but I set a condition for myself: I would not leave until I heard at least one song I recognized...

The last song I managed to catch (before tearing myself away) went: 'Beauty is a terrible force, and I know no words to speak of it!'

With the chorus repeated thrice, I bolted from the church building with my suitcase, its wheels clattering against the pavement. It was time for me to go. Asking for directions from the first passerby I met, I dove into the labyrinth of the subway.

I missed my train (and, of course, fell into a panic)—it had departed a minute before my arrival; in the end, I did reach my destination after all. But, in truth, I do not regret leaving the concert early—I enjoyed wandering aimlessly through the corridors of fate...
